verses.text: Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother,

Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours:
Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.
I thank my God always on your behalf, for the grace of God which is given you by Jesus Christ;
That in every thing ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge;
Even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you:
So that ye come behind in no gift; waiting for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ:
Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
For it hath been declared unto me of you, my brethren, by them which are of the house of Chloe, that there are contentions among you.
Now this I say, that every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ.
Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?
I thank God that I baptized none of you, but Crispus and Gaius;
Lest any should say that I had baptized in mine own name.
And I baptized also the household of Stephanas: besides, I know not whether I baptized any other.
For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect.
For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.
For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent.
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom:
But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God.
Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are:
That no flesh should glory in his presence.
But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption:
That, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.

chapters.summary: Paul opens with his credentials and a co-sender — "Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother" — and writes "Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints," immediately widening the address to "all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours," so that a quarrelling congregation is never permitted to think of itself in isolation. The thanksgiving that follows is generous and, read against the rest of the letter, pointed: he thanks God "for the grace of God which is given you by Jesus Christ," that "in every thing ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge," and that "ye come behind in no gift; waiting for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." These are the very endowments the Corinthians will shortly be rebuked for mishandling, yet Paul names them as gifts before he names them as problems, and he grounds their perseverance not in their gifting but in the God "Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ," summing it up in four words of assurance: "God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord." Then the trouble surfaces. "Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment." The report has come "by them which are of the house of Chloe, that there are contentions among you," and the contentions have hardened into slogans of allegiance: "every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ." Paul answers with three questions that demolish all four parties at once — "Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?" — and is relieved to have personally baptized so few of them, "none of you, but Crispus and Gaius" and "the household of Stephanas," precisely "Lest any should say that I had baptized in mine own name." He then states the shape of his own commission: "For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect." That last clause opens the chapter's great argument, and the argument is about the cross rather than about church politics. "For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God." Scripture had already announced the reversal — "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent" — so Paul taunts the recognized authorities of the age: "Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?" The strategy behind the reversal is deliberate: "after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe." Both halves of Paul's world are scandalized by the result, since "the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom: But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; But unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God. Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Finally Paul turns the lens on the congregation itself as the standing evidence of his case: "ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty; And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are." The purpose is stated without softening — "That no flesh should glory in his presence" — and the only permitted alternative is Christ himself, "who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption: That, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord."
takeaways: Paul thanks God for the Corinthians before he corrects them, and what he thanks God for is exactly what they have abused. They are "enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge" and "come behind in no gift," yet the whole letter will show a church that is gifted and immature at the same time. The chapter therefore refuses the assumption that spiritual endowment is spiritual maturity: eloquence, knowledge, and charism are real gifts of grace and are no proof at all that the people holding them are walking rightly. Correction begins by acknowledging what God has genuinely given, not by denying it.

The security Paul offers is placed entirely outside the Corinthians themselves. It is God "Who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ," and the ground of that confidence is stated as a bare fact about God rather than about them: "God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord." A church that has just been described as full of contentions is told that its future blamelessness rests on divine fidelity, which is both the strongest possible comfort and the strongest possible rebuke to factional self-confidence.

The party slogans are treated as a single disease rather than three good options and one bad one. "I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ" — and the fourth slogan, which sounds unimpeachable, is listed alongside the others as one more banner in a fight. The three questions that follow expose what a party spirit actually claims: "Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?" No teacher was crucified for the church and no one was baptized into a teacher's name, so attaching one's identity to a human leader is a quiet theft of what belongs to Christ alone.

"For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel" is a statement about Paul's particular commission, not a ranking of baptism as unimportant, and the sentence itself proves it, since Paul carefully recalls whom he did baptize and why he is glad the number was small: "Lest any should say that I had baptized in mine own name." His concern is that the rite not become a personal loyalty badge. The reason given for preaching "not with wisdom of words" is likewise practical rather than anti-intellectual: rhetorical brilliance can so absorb the hearer's admiration that "the cross of Christ should be made of none effect," the message swallowed by the medium.

The cross divides humanity by what it looks like to them: "the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God." Paul names the two standing objections of his world with precision — "the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom" — and answers both with the same offensive content, "Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness." He does not soften the offense but relocates it, because to "them which are called" that identical crucified Christ is "the power of God, and the wisdom of God." The gospel is not a sign for the sign-seekers and a philosophy for the philosophers; it is one scandal that becomes power in those who are called.

The Corinthian membership roll is itself the argument: "not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise... and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are." God's choosing runs deliberately against every metric of status, and the stated purpose is the elimination of boasting — "That no flesh should glory in his presence." The chapter then closes by naming what replaces the boast, since Christ "of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption." Everything the factions were competing over is already given in one person, which is why the only remaining option is that "He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord."

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 29:14 — the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid
crossRefs.why: Paul's "For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent" draws directly on this oracle, where God answers a people who honour him "with their lips" while their heart is far from him. Reading the source shows that the overturning of human wisdom is not a new emergency measure taken at Calvary but God's long-standing way of dealing with religion that has become expert and hollow.

crossRefs.label: Jeremiah 9:23-24 — Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might
crossRefs.why: The chapter's closing line, "He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord," is quoted from this passage, and the original names the same three boasts Paul has just dismissed among the Corinthians: wisdom, might, and wealth or nobility. The prophet's alternative — glorying in knowing God — explains why Paul answers the boast not with humility as a mood but with a person, Christ "made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption."

crossRefs.label: Acts 18 — And Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed on the Lord with all his house
crossRefs.why: Luke supplies the history standing behind the names in this chapter: Paul's eighteen months at Corinth, the conversion of Crispus and his household, Gaius the host, and Sosthenes the synagogue ruler beaten before the judgment seat, who is plausibly the "Sosthenes our brother" now co-sending the letter. The narrative also shows Paul arriving at Corinth from Athens, which gives concrete weight to his refusal of "wisdom of words" in a city so near the philosophers.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 3 — while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?
crossRefs.why: Paul returns to the same slogans two chapters later and supplies the diagnosis and the remedy that chapter one only announces: the parties are evidence of carnality, and the leaders they idolize are merely servants, since "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." The two chapters together move the argument from "Is Christ divided?" to a positive account of what ministers actually are.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 6:14 — God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ
crossRefs.why: Paul states there as personal resolve what he argues here as theology, and in a setting where rivals sought a following by an impressive external mark. The parallel confirms that the ban on glorying in this chapter is not a general lesson in modesty but a specific refusal to let anything other than the cross function as the church's boast or its badge of belonging.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 11:25 — thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes
crossRefs.why: Jesus rejoices over the identical pattern Paul describes: revelation withheld from the credentialed and given to those with no standing, and this by the Father's good pleasure rather than by accident. Set beside "it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe," the saying shows that Paul is not inventing a Corinthian paradox but restating the way the kingdom had been arriving from the beginning.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel," the Catholic reading takes Paul to be distinguishing his own apostolic priority from the administration of a rite, not lowering the rite itself. Baptism in this reading genuinely effects what it signifies, incorporating a person into Christ, which is exactly why Paul is anxious that no one be able to say "that I had baptized in mine own name": if baptism were a bare token of personal allegiance the danger of factional branding would be trivial, but because it truly makes a person Christ's, attaching it to a human name is a serious distortion. Catholic readers also note that Paul baptizes "the household of Stephanas" as a unit, and take household baptism as consistent with the Church's practice of baptizing whole families including those unable to profess faith for themselves.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings split here. Baptist and broadly evangelical interpreters read the plain subordination — sent "not to baptize, but to preach" — as showing that baptism is an ordinance that signifies and seals a salvation already received through the preached word, not a rite that conveys grace by its performance; on this view Paul's relief at having baptized so few would be strange if baptism itself were the moment of new birth. They also hold that a household mention establishes nothing about infants, since the same household is later described as devoting itself to ministry. Reformed and Lutheran paedobaptists agree with much of the Catholic reading of the household and of baptism's efficacy while still locating its power in the promise received by faith rather than in the act as such. All sides agree Paul's actual target is factionalism, and that he assumes every Corinthian believer has been baptized.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads "of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption" as a single unbroken gift in which righteousness and sanctification are not separable stages but aspects of one real union with Christ. Being "sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints" is therefore taken as an actual change in the person, a righteousness truly given and truly making the believer holy, which is then lived out and can be grown in or lost. The chapter's opening description of the Corinthians as already sanctified while still full of contentions is read as the tension of a holiness genuinely received and not yet fully realized in conduct.

counterpoint.summary: Classical Protestant readings take the same verse as the clearest possible statement that righteousness is not produced in us but given to us in Christ, received by faith and reckoned to the believer rather than infused as a quality. On this view Paul's list is deliberately Christ-centred: wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption are all located in a person outside ourselves, so that the ground of standing before God can never become a personal achievement — which is precisely the point of "That no flesh should glory in his presence." Protestant interpreters typically distinguish justification, complete and immediate, from sanctification as the ongoing work that follows, and read the address to contentious "saints" as proof that status before God is not measured by present performance. Both traditions insist that all four gifts are Christ's and none of them are self-generated.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading hears in "that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment" a call to visible, structural unity, not merely inward goodwill. The named parties are attached to concrete apostolic figures, and the remedy Paul assumes is a common teaching and a common communion that can actually be identified, so the verse is read as supporting the conviction that the Church's oneness must be discernible in doctrine, worship, and governance rather than existing only in an invisible fellowship of believers.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally agree the command is strong and that ordinary denominational division falls short of it, but locate the unity Paul demands in shared confession of the crucified Christ rather than in a single institutional structure. They note that Paul's corrective is entirely christological — "Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you?" — and that he does not appeal to an office or a jurisdiction to settle the quarrel but to the cross and to the gospel he preached. On this reading the church's essential oneness is given in Christ and is expressed, imperfectly, wherever that gospel is confessed. Both traditions read the passage as a rebuke to partisanship built on personalities rather than on Christ.

verses.text: And I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God.
For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling.
And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.
Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought:
But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory:
Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.
But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit: for the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God.
For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.
Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God.
Which things also we speak, not in the words which man’s wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual.
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man.
For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ.

chapters.summary: Having just argued that God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, Paul turns the argument on himself and offers his own arrival at Corinth as the proof. "And I, brethren, when I came to you, came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God." In a city that priced rhetoric and paid well for it, he came with a deliberately narrowed subject — "For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified" — and by his own account he was no impressive figure while he did it: "And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling." The manner matched the message. His "speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man’s wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power," and he names the reason without hedging: "That your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God." A faith produced by a persuasive speaker rests on that speaker, and falls when he is outargued. Then Paul guards himself against being misheard as despising thought altogether. "Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought." There is a wisdom, but it belongs to another order: "we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory." Its hiddenness is proved by the crucifixion itself — "Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory" — so that the powers who arranged the cross were, in that very act, walking into the plan they meant to defeat. What no eye discovered, God disclosed: "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him. But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit." The last third grounds all of this in the Spirit’s own competence. "The Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God," and Paul argues from the analogy of self-knowledge: as "the things of a man" are known only by "the spirit of man which is in him," so "the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God." Believers have "received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God," and the teaching that carries this gift is in kind with it, "not in the words which man’s wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual." Hence the impasse the whole chapter has been circling: "the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned." Paul ends with a prophet’s unanswerable question and an answer that should not exist: "For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ."
takeaways: Paul handicaps his own presentation on purpose, and he tells us why. He "came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom" and refused "enticing words of man’s wisdom" so "that your faith should not stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God." The reasoning is pastoral rather than aesthetic: whatever wins a hearer is what holds him, so a faith argued into place by brilliance is only as durable as the next, more brilliant argument. By stripping the delivery, Paul makes the foundation visible, and the question he forces on every preacher and teacher after him is not whether their case is compelling but what their hearers will finally be resting on.

"For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified" is a decision about content, not a boast about ignorance. It is also not a beginner’s topic later outgrown, because when Paul goes on to speak "wisdom among them that are perfect," the wisdom he names is "the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory" — the same crucified Lord seen at depth. Christian maturity in this chapter is not moving on from the cross to something more advanced; it is being taken further into what was there from the beginning.

The chapter sets Paul’s condition and the effect of his preaching side by side without embarrassment: he was "in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling," and yet his preaching was "in demonstration of the Spirit and of power." The juxtaposition is the argument. Had the speaker been formidable, the power could plausibly have been credited to him; because he was not, the demonstration had to be attributed elsewhere. This is why weakness in ministry is treated here as evidence rather than as an obstacle to be apologized for or engineered away.

The most chilling line in the chapter is a claim about competence: "Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." Worldly power at its most decisive was at its most blind, and it executed the plan it was trying to stop. Paul has already said such wisdom and such rulers "come to nought," so the verdict is not that the world’s expertise is merely second-rate but that it is on a trajectory toward nothing. Every confident judgment made without the Spirit stands under the possibility of being that catastrophically wrong.

"Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man" is often quoted as a sigh about how little we can know, but Paul’s next word overturns it: "But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit." The three avenues named — sight, hearing, imagination — cover the whole range of human discovery, and all three come up empty; the knowledge arrives instead as self-disclosure, because only "the Spirit of God" knows "the things of God" the way a man’s own spirit knows "the things of a man." Revelation here is not humanity climbing to a conclusion but God opening his own interior life to those he loves.

"The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned" explains why the same gospel lands as power on one hearer and absurdity on another, and it removes any grounds for smugness in those who believe, since what they have is something "freely given to us of God." Note also the grammar of the conclusion: it is "we have the mind of Christ," not I. The discernment Paul claims, and the statement that "he that is spiritual judgeth all things," is spoken in the plural to a congregation he is in the middle of correcting — a possession of the body, not a private trump card to be played against it.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 64:4 — neither hath the eye seen, O God, beside thee, what he hath prepared for him that waiteth for him
crossRefs.why: Paul’s "as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard" reaches back to a prophet pleading for God to tear open the heavens and come down. Isaiah’s point is that no one has ever discovered what God has in store; Paul quotes it and then answers it, since "God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit." Reading the two together shows the chapter is not celebrating mystery for its own sake but announcing that the long wait has ended.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 40:13 — Who hath directed the Spirit of the LORD, or being his counsellor hath taught him?
crossRefs.why: The closing question, "who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him?", is lifted from a passage where it is deliberately unanswerable, asserting that God is beyond all counsel and comparison. Paul does not soften the question; he lets it stand and then says "But we have the mind of Christ." The shock of the verse only registers when the reader hears the prophet’s original intent behind it.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 1:23-25 — we preach Christ crucified... the foolishness of God is wiser than men
crossRefs.why: Chapter two is the autobiographical demonstration of the thesis stated just before it. Having argued that God saves by what the world calls foolishness and chooses the weak "to confound the things which are mighty," Paul now shows the principle enacted in his own arrival "in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling." The two chapters should be read as one continuous argument rather than as a doctrine followed by an anecdote.

crossRefs.label: Acts 18:9-10 — Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace
crossRefs.why: Luke’s account of the founding visit supplies the circumstances behind Paul’s memory of preaching "in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling": a hostile synagogue, a move next door, and a night vision telling him not to be afraid because God had "much people in this city." The narrative confirms that the fear Paul admits to was real and situational, not a rhetorical pose adopted for the letter.

crossRefs.label: John 16:13-14 — when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth
crossRefs.why: The Spirit who "searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God" is the Spirit promised in the upper room, who "shall not speak of himself" but "shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you." Both passages make the Spirit the internal condition of understanding rather than an extra source of information, and both anchor his teaching to Christ, which keeps "the hidden wisdom" from drifting into open-ended novelty.

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 5:14 — strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised
crossRefs.why: Paul’s aside that "we speak wisdom among them that are perfect" assumes a maturity capable of receiving more, and Hebrews describes the same distinction as milk against strong meat, with discernment developed by practice. Catholic spiritual theology in particular has read these passages together as describing real stages of growth in the interior life, where deeper understanding follows formation rather than mere information.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God... neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned" as a statement about the necessity of grace for supernatural faith rather than about the total extinction of human reason. Fallen nature is understood as genuinely wounded but not annihilated, so that reason can still reach real truths about God and the moral order while remaining wholly incapable of the mysteries "which God ordained before the world unto our glory." Grace is therefore required to begin, sustain, and complete faith; but once it is given, the person truly cooperates with it, and "the natural man" names the human being left to his own resources rather than one incapable of any response when grace is offered.

counterpoint.summary: Reformed interpreters press the verse harder, reading "neither can he know them" as a statement of real inability that extends to the mind itself, so that regeneration by the Spirit must precede and produce faith rather than merely assist a capacity already present; on this reading the illumination described here is closer to being given new life than to having existing sight improved, and accounts of cooperation are thought to understate the flat "can not." Wesleyan and Arminian readings stand nearer the Catholic account, holding that grace goes before and enables a response that remains genuinely free. All sides agree that spiritual understanding is a gift and not an achievement, and that nothing in this chapter allows a believer to credit his own insight for what he has received "freely... of God."

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds in "we speak wisdom among them that are perfect... the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom" a warrant for real depth within the one deposit of faith, unfolded over time and delivered to those being formed. "Mystery" here is understood less as a puzzle awaiting solution than as a reality to be entered, which is why the same word governs the Church’s sacramental life; and the address to "them that are perfect" is read as recognizing degrees of maturity, so that catechesis leads into deeper initiation rather than repeating an introduction. On this reading, growth in understanding is handed on within the communion of the Church, and the development of doctrine is the same wisdom penetrated more deeply, never a new revelation added to it.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters are wary of anything resembling a two-tier gospel or a reserve of teaching held back from ordinary believers, and they note that Paul defines his mystery within the chapter itself: it is the crucified "Lord of glory," publicly preached, whose hiddenness lay in the blindness of "the princes of this world" rather than in any policy of concealment. "Them that are perfect" is taken to mean the mature, a description of believers who have grown rather than an inner circle, and since the Spirit who "searcheth all things" is given to all who believe, the depth Paul speaks of is available to the whole congregation. Development is affirmed as clarification of what Scripture already contains rather than as an unfolding that could yield content Scripture does not hold. Both traditions agree that the wisdom in question is Christ crucified and that it cannot be reached by natural insight.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man," Catholic reading resists taking the verse as a charter for private judgment set against the Church. The whole passage is written in the plural — believers "have received... the spirit which is of God," and the conclusion is "we have the mind of Christ" — and it is addressed to a congregation Paul is in the middle of correcting precisely because rival parties there each claimed spiritual standing. Discernment is therefore understood as belonging to the body: exercised by pastors charged with teaching and carried also in the whole faithful’s instinct for the faith, so that the spiritual person judges rightly within the communion that formed him rather than over against it.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings take the verse as grounding the competence of every Spirit-indwelt believer to read Scripture and weigh what is taught, since the discernment described is tied to having "received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God" and not to any office. This underwrites both the priesthood of all believers and the conviction that Scripture is clear enough on what matters most for the ordinary Christian to judge teaching by it, with the further point that the natural man’s inability to assess spiritual things means the Church’s message will always be unintelligible to those who evaluate it on worldly terms. Careful Protestant interpreters add that the plural is real and that such judgment is meant to be exercised with the congregation and tested against the shared confession, not as private license. Both traditions agree that discernment is a gift of the Spirit rather than a natural talent, and that Paul is not authorizing an individualism detached from the body.

verses.text: And I, brethren, could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ.
I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it, neither yet now are ye able.
For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men?
For while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?
Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man?
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase.
Now he that planteth and he that watereth are one: and every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour.
For we are labourers together with God: ye are God’s husbandry, ye are God’s building.
According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon.
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble;
Every man’s work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is.
If any man’s work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward.
If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.
Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?
If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are.
Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
And again, The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain.
Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are yours;
Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours;
And ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s.

chapters.summary: Paul has already named the Corinthian factions; here he diagnoses them. He tells them he "could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ," having fed them "with milk, and not with meat" because they were not able to bear it — "neither yet now are ye able." The proof of their infancy is not ignorance of doctrine but the temper of their common life: "whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men?" Party slogans are the symptom, and Paul takes the first of them as his own indictment: "while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?" His answer deflates both names at once — "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man?" — and then supplies the image that governs the rest of the chapter: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." Because growth belongs to God, "neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth," yet the workers are not thereby erased; they "are one," and "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour." The field turns into a construction site: "ye are God’s husbandry, ye are God’s building." Paul describes himself as "a wise masterbuilder" who has "laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon," with a warning attached — "let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon" — since "other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." What is built on that foundation will be sorted by fire: some raise "gold, silver, precious stones," others "wood, hay, stubble," and "the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is." Work that abides earns "a reward"; work that burns means real loss, "but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire." The building then proves to be a sanctuary: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" — and the party spirit tearing at that community is no small matter, for "if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are." Paul closes by inverting the very thing the factions were competing over. "Let no man deceive himself. If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise," because "the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God," as the scriptures testify: "He taketh the wise in their own craftiness," and "The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain." The conclusion turns their arithmetic inside out — they had been dividing themselves up among teachers, when in fact "all things are yours; Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours; And ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s."
takeaways: Spiritual maturity is measured here by how a community behaves, not by how much it knows. Paul calls the Corinthians "carnal" and "babes in Christ" and names the evidence plainly: "envying, and strife, and divisions." They are not accused of heresy or immorality at this point, only of factionalism — which turns out to be enough. To "walk as men" is to run a church by the ordinary logic of rival loyalties and personalities, and Paul treats that as a diet problem: people still on "milk, and not with meat" cannot digest the deeper teaching, and the reason is moral rather than intellectual.

The chapter dismantles celebrity ministry without dismissing ministers. "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed" strips the names of any claim to be sources; "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" locates all fruitfulness in God alone. Yet the same passage refuses to make the workers irrelevant: they "are one," not competitors, they are "labourers together with God," and "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour." Genuine human effort is real and will be genuinely rewarded, precisely because it is not the cause of the growth and therefore has nothing to protect.

There is exactly one foundation and unlimited responsibility for what is raised on it. "Other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ" closes the question of the church’s basis permanently, but that settled foundation makes the next sentence more urgent rather than less: "let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon." The contrast between "gold, silver, precious stones" and "wood, hay, stubble" is not a contrast between true and false religion — all of it is built on Christ — but between work that survives testing and work that does not. Being on the right foundation is no guarantee of building well.

Judgment is described as revelation before it is described as punishment. "Every man’s work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire; and the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is." The fire is an assayer, not primarily an executioner; its function is to show "of what sort" the work is. And the outcome for the builder whose work fails is stated with striking restraint — "he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire." Real loss and real salvation are held together in a single verse, which is why this text has carried so much weight in later argument about what happens to a saved person’s unworthy work.

The community itself is the sanctuary, and damaging it is sacrilege. "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" is addressed to a whole congregation in the plural, so the temple in view is the assembled church before it is the individual believer. That is what raises the stakes of mere partisanship to "If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy." Faction-building is not a matter of poor manners in a voluntary society; it is defacing a holy place, and the reason given is simply what the place is: "the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are."

The remedy for competitive wisdom is a deliberate self-emptying. "If any man among you seemeth to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise" asks for a real surrender of standing, not a rhetorical pose, and it is grounded in a verdict already rendered: "the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." The chapter’s final turn then exposes how small the factions had made themselves. In claiming a teacher they had been dividing an inheritance that was already entirely theirs — "all things are yours; Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come" — and the whole chain is anchored where boasting cannot reach: "ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s."

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 1:10-31 — every one of you saith, I am of Paul... but God hath chosen the foolish things of the world
crossRefs.why: The opening chapter states the problem this one diagnoses: the same slogans, the same names, and the same collision between "the wisdom of this world" and the preaching of a crucified Christ. Read together, the two chapters show that Paul treats Corinthian factionalism and Corinthian admiration for clever speech as a single disorder, which is why he answers party spirit with a doctrine of God-given increase rather than with a compromise between the parties.

crossRefs.label: Acts 18 — Paul... continued there a year and six months... and Apollos... mightily convinced the Jews
crossRefs.why: Luke supplies the history behind "I have planted, Apollos watered." Paul founded the Corinthian congregation over eighteen months, and the eloquent Alexandrian arrived afterward and helped the believers greatly. Knowing that both men actually worked in sequence rather than in rivalry sharpens Paul’s point that the factions had invented a competition their supposed champions never had.

crossRefs.label: Job 5:13 — He taketh the wise in their own craftiness
crossRefs.why: Paul quotes this line directly as scriptural proof that "the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God." The original setting is a speech about God overturning the schemes of the crafty and lifting the lowly, which is the same reversal Paul is applying to Corinthian factions built on admiration for skilled speakers.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 2:19-22 — built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone... an holy temple in the Lord
crossRefs.why: The same two images — foundation and temple — are joined there as here, with the building described as growing into "an habitation of God through the Spirit." The parallel confirms that Paul’s "ye are God’s building" and "ye are the temple of God" describe one corporate structure made of people, and it clarifies how the apostolic foundation-laying of this chapter relates to Christ as the foundation itself.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 5:10 — we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body
crossRefs.why: Paul later states as bare doctrine what he here dramatizes with fire and building materials: believers are assessed for what they have done. Set beside "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour" and "the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is," it establishes that a judgment of works applies to the saved and not only to the lost.

crossRefs.label: Malachi 3:2-3 — for he is like a refiner’s fire... and he shall purify the sons of Levi
crossRefs.why: The prophet describes the Lord’s coming to his temple as a refining that purges rather than destroys, so that offerings may be made "in righteousness." Catholic reading hears that refining note in "the day shall declare it, because it shall be revealed by fire" and especially in "he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire," where the person passes through the fire and comes out purified rather than condemned.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds in "If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire" one of the clearest scriptural pointers toward a purification after death. The person in view is neither condemned nor waved through: he is saved, yet he genuinely suffers loss, and he passes through fire to arrive there. Since the fire is said to "try every man’s work of what sort it is" and the deficient work is destroyed while the builder survives, the tradition reads the passage as describing a real purgative experience for those who die in grace but with attachments and unworthy work still clinging to them. Set alongside the chapter’s temple language — "the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are" — the argument is that holiness is not merely imputed at the threshold but actually completed, and that this passage shows the completing as costly.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the fire here as the eschatological judgment of Christ’s appearing rather than an intermediate state. The stated subject of the testing is the work, not the worker — "the fire shall try every man’s work of what sort it is" — and "the day shall declare it" points to a single public day of assessment, so the loss described is the loss of reward for ministry poorly built, not a period of personal expiation. The phrase "yet so as by fire" is taken as an image of narrow escape, like a man running out of a burning house with nothing but his life, which underlines that his salvation rests wholly on the one foundation already laid and not on the quality of what he built. Both traditions agree that the believer is truly saved, that the loss is real, and that the entire scene presupposes salvation grounded in Christ rather than in the surviving work.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic reading, "For we are labourers together with God" states a genuine cooperation between divine grace and human action, and the chapter holds that cooperation in balance rather than resolving it in one direction. God alone "gave the increase," so no minister is a source of anything; and yet "every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour," which presupposes that the labour is truly the man’s own and truly counts. Catholic tradition takes this as the shape of merit: what is rewarded is God’s grace at work in a free human agent, so that crediting the reward to the labourer and crediting the growth to God are not competing claims. The ministers are read as real instrumental causes — "ministers by whom ye believed" — through whom God ordinarily gives what only he can give.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters emphasize the negative half of the same argument, where Paul says that "neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase." On this reading the point of the planting-and-watering image is to reduce the workers to nothing precisely so that boasting in men becomes impossible — "therefore let no man glory in men" — and the rewards that follow are understood as God graciously crowning his own gifts rather than as wages the labourer has earned. The distinction usually drawn is between reward, which this chapter clearly promises to believers, and merit understood as a claim on God, which Protestants deny while affirming that works done in faith are truly assessed and truly rewarded. Both traditions affirm that God alone gives growth, that ministers are instruments rather than sources, and that faithful labour is not wasted.

verses.text: Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man’s judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self.
For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord.

Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God.

And these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another.
For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us: and I would to God ye did reign, that we also might reign with you.
For I think that God hath set forth us the apostles last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men.
We are fools for Christ’s sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised.
Even unto this present hour we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace;
And labour, working with our own hands: being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it:
Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day.
I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you.
For though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel.
Wherefore I beseech you, be ye followers of me.

For this cause have I sent unto you Timotheus, who is my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord, who shall bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church.
Now some are puffed up, as though I would not come to you.
But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and will know, not the speech of them which are puffed up, but the power.
For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power.
What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?

chapters.summary: Paul closes his argument against the Corinthian party spirit by fixing the apostles in their proper place: "Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God." A steward owns nothing and answers to his master, so only one demand is made of him — "Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful." That single standard dissolves the habit of ranking teachers, and Paul refuses the Corinthians' verdict and even his own: "with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man’s judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self." A clean conscience settles nothing, since "I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord." The real verdict waits — "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God." Paul then names his method, that "these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another," and drives at the root of the factions with three questions: "who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?" Everything they boast in arrived as a gift, so the boasting is incoherent. Irony follows — "Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us: and I would to God ye did reign, that we also might reign with you" — and against that imagined enthronement Paul sets the apostles' actual position, "last, as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men." The contrast is laid out in pairs: "We are fools for Christ’s sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised." The catalogue that follows is physical and unglamorous — they "hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace," they "labour, working with our own hands," and their response to hostility reverses it: "being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it: Being defamed, we intreat," until they are "made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day." Then the tone turns paternal. "I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you. For though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel." On that ground alone he can say "be ye followers of me," and he sends Timotheus, "my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord," to "bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church." To those "puffed up, as though I would not come to you," he promises a visit that will test substance rather than rhetoric: "I will come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and will know, not the speech of them which are puffed up, but the power. For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power." The chapter ends by handing them the choice: "What will ye? shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?"
takeaways: Ministry is defined here by stewardship rather than by ownership or celebrity. Paul asks only that he be accounted one of "the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God," and a steward is by definition handling what belongs to someone else. That is why the measure applied to him is not eloquence, results, or popularity but a single quality — "it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful." The Corinthians were grading their teachers like patrons grading orators; Paul answers that the goods were never his to be praised for, and that the only relevant question about a steward is whether he was true to the master's intent with the master's property.

The chapter installs a deliberate reserve about verdicts, including verdicts on oneself. Paul treats the church's opinion of him as "a very small thing," and then goes further: "yea, I judge not mine own self. For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified." A quiet conscience is evidence, not acquittal, because self-knowledge is partial and the court is not one's own. The instruction that follows — "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come" — is not a ban on discernment, since Paul issues sharp judgments a chapter later, but a ban on premature final verdicts about persons whose hidden motives only God can read. Notably, the outcome he expects from that disclosure is generous: "then shall every man have praise of God."

The three questions of verse seven cut the nerve of every rivalry in the letter: "who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?" Paul does not deny that the Corinthians have real gifts, real teachers, and real knowledge. He denies that any of it originated with them. Boasting in a gift is a category error, treating a received thing as an achievement, and once that is seen, being "puffed up for one against another" collapses on its own without needing any further argument.

Paul's irony exposes a church that thinks it has already arrived. "Now ye are full, now ye are rich, ye have reigned as kings without us" describes a community living as though the age of glory had come early, and his wistful reply — "I would to God ye did reign, that we also might reign with you" — concedes the hope while denying the timing. The apostolic reality is the opposite shape: "last, as it were appointed to death," a "spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men," hungry, homeless, "the offscouring of all things." The pattern of authentic ministry is cruciform, and the sign of it is the reversal in their conduct — "being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it: Being defamed, we intreat."

Against a market of teachers Paul asserts a relationship that cannot be duplicated: "though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel." Instruction can be shopped for, but the one through whom the gospel first gave them life stands in a different relation entirely, which is why he can follow it with "be ye followers of me" without arrogance. The fatherhood is exercised as warning rather than shaming — "I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you" — and it is handed on through a person, Timotheus, who will "bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church." The content taught at Corinth is not a local variant but the same teaching given everywhere.

The closing test is between talk and reality: "I will come to you shortly, if the Lord will, and will know, not the speech of them which are puffed up, but the power. For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power." In a city that prized rhetorical display, Paul says the kingdom will be audited by what it actually effects, not by how impressively it is described. The final question leaves the outcome with the Corinthians rather than with him — "shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?" — so that even apostolic discipline is presented as something their own response determines.

crossRefs.label: Luke 12:42-48 — Who then is that faithful and wise steward... to give them their portion of meat in due season?
crossRefs.why: The parable supplies the picture Paul is working from when he calls the apostles "stewards of the mysteries of God" and insists "it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful." A steward is judged at the master's return, not by the household's opinion in the meantime, which is exactly why Paul can say "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come."

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 3:6-7,21 — I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase... let no man glory in men
crossRefs.why: Chapter four is the conclusion of an argument begun here, where the same pair of names is used to make the same point. The planting and watering image already reduces the teachers to instruments, and "let no man glory in men" is what verse seven then presses to its root with "what hast thou that thou didst not receive?"

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 11:23-27 — in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent... in hunger and thirst
crossRefs.why: The later catalogue of hardships expands the one given here in compressed form: "we both hunger, and thirst, and are naked, and are buffeted, and have no certain dwellingplace." In both places Paul answers rivals who trade on impressive appearance by listing what looks like disqualification, treating weakness as the credential of a true apostle.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 7:1-2 — Judge not, that ye be not judged
crossRefs.why: Paul's "judge nothing before the time" is often read alongside this saying, and the pairing clarifies both. Neither text forbids discernment, since Paul commands a hard judgment in the very next chapter of this letter; what both forbid is the presumption of rendering a final verdict on a person, which belongs to the one "who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts."

crossRefs.label: Galatians 4:19 — My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you
crossRefs.why: The same paternal language appears there under a maternal image, showing that Paul's claim "in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" is a settled way of describing his relation to churches he founded, not a one-time rhetorical flourish. Both passages combine deep affection with the willingness to rebuke that affection makes possible.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 23:8-9 — call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven
crossRefs.why: This saying is the standing counterweight to Paul's "ye have not many fathers," and the two texts are the poles of a long dispute over spiritual paternity and titles. Read together they frame the question of whether Paul is claiming something the Lord forbade or exercising a derived fatherhood that points past itself, since his own point is that he begot them only "through the gospel."

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading hears in "stewards of the mysteries of God" a description of the ordained ministry as an entrusted office, and takes the "mysteries" to include the sacraments as well as the revealed saving plan. On this reading Paul is not describing every believer's stewardship of the gospel in general but the particular dispensation committed to those set apart as "the ministers of Christ," who administer holy things that are not their own property and who will answer to the Lord and not to the congregation for how they have handled them. The requirement "that a man be found faithful" is then read as attaching to an office with real authority — the same authority that allows Paul to speak of coming "with a rod" — while the office itself remains wholly instrumental, since the mysteries belong to God.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take "the mysteries of God" here in continuity with Paul's earlier use in this letter, where the mystery is the hidden wisdom of God now revealed in the crucified Christ, so that stewardship means above all the faithful preaching and safeguarding of that gospel. On this reading the accent falls on the word entrusted rather than on sacramental administration, ministers are servants of that word rather than holders of a sacerdotal office, and the whole passage cuts against clerical status precisely by describing ministers as dispensable stewards of goods belonging to another. Both traditions agree that the minister owns nothing he dispenses, that his accountability runs to the Lord rather than to the congregation's estimate, and that fidelity rather than impressiveness is the only measure that will finally count.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic tradition reads "in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" as establishing a genuine spiritual fatherhood, exercised in the Church and derived entirely from God's own fatherhood. Paul distinguishes the many "instructers" from the few "fathers," which implies that teaching alone does not create the bond he has with the Corinthians; something generative happened through his ministry of the gospel that gives him both the right to say "be ye followers of me" and the standing to warn them "as my beloved sons." This is the scriptural warrant traditionally invoked for calling those in pastoral office fathers, on the understanding that the title always names a participation in the Father's paternity rather than a rival to it.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers point to the Lord's own instruction to "call no man your father upon the earth," and argue that Paul is using an affectionate metaphor for a unique historical relation — he personally founded this church — rather than authorizing an ecclesiastical title. They note that Paul immediately qualifies the claim by grounding it in the gospel itself, that he elsewhere insists neither he nor Apollos is anything, and that the chapter's whole thrust is against elevating human figures, which makes it an odd basis for a permanent honorific. Both traditions affirm that whatever fatherhood Paul claims is derivative and instrumental, that imitation of a minister is legitimate only so far as he imitates Christ, and that the relationship is meant to produce maturity rather than dependence.

interpretationNotes.claim: On the Catholic reading, "not to think of men above that which is written" is a warning against the Corinthians' inflated estimate of their favorite teachers, measured by the scriptural texts Paul has already been citing against human boasting, rather than a formal principle that written Scripture alone is the rule of faith. The immediate object of the phrase is men, not doctrine: the Corinthians are to stop rating Paul and Apollos beyond what the written word allows anyone to claim for a mere servant. The same chapter is read as showing how apostolic teaching was actually transmitted, since Paul sends Timotheus to "bring you into remembrance of my ways which be in Christ, as I teach every where in every church" — a living, personally carried, and uniform apostolic practice held across all the churches.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters read the phrase as placing a written standard over every human estimate, and take it as an early expression of the instinct that Scripture norms the Church's judgments rather than the reverse. They observe that Paul appeals to what is written as the fixed measure at precisely the moment he is dismantling loyalty to personalities, and that his own oral teaching is not set against Scripture but is the apostolic message that would itself be inscribed, so that the "ways which be in Christ" delivered uniformly to every church are the same content now available in the apostolic writings. Both traditions agree that Paul subordinates all human teachers to a standard outside themselves, and that the practical aim of the verse is that "no one of you be puffed up for one against another."
