verses.text: Am I not an apostle? am I not free? have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? are not ye my work in the Lord?
If I be not an apostle unto others, yet doubtless I am to you: for the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord.
Mine answer to them that do examine me is this,
Have we not power to eat and to drink?
Have we not power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas?
Or I only and Barnabas, have not we power to forbear working?
Who goeth a warfare any time at his own charges? who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not of the fruit thereof? or who feedeth a flock, and eateth not of the milk of the flock?
Say I these things as a man? or saith not the law the same also?
For it is written in the law of Moses, Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn. Doth God take care for oxen?
Or saith he it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, this is written: that he that ploweth should plow in hope; and that he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope.
If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things?
If others be partakers of this power over you, are not we rather? Nevertheless we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ.
Do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar?
Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.
But I have used none of these things: neither have I written these things, that it should be so done unto me: for it were better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void.
For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!
For if I do this thing willingly, I have a reward: but if against my will, a dispensation of the gospel is committed unto me.
What is my reward then? Verily that, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge, that I abuse not my power in the gospel.
For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more.
And unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to them that are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain them that are under the law;
To them that are without law, as without law, ( being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ,) that I might gain them that are without law.
To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.
And this I do for the gospel’s sake, that I might be partaker thereof with you.
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air:
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.

chapters.summary: Having just told the Corinthians that he would eat no flesh forever rather than wound a weak brother, Paul now turns the argument on himself and makes his own life the demonstration. He opens with four questions fired off in a row — "Am I not an apostle? am I not free? have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? are not ye my work in the Lord?" — and tells them that whatever others may say, "the seal of mine apostleship are ye in the Lord." "Mine answer to them that do examine me is this," he says, and then, instead of defending his rights, he catalogues them at length so that laying them down will cost something visible. Has he not "power to eat and to drink"? "power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas"? Are he and Barnabas alone required to keep working with their hands? He argues from ordinary life — "Who goeth a warfare any time at his own charges? who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not of the fruit thereof? or who feedeth a flock, and eateth not of the milk of the flock?" — then from the law of Moses, "Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn," pressing the question "Doth God take care for oxen? Or saith he it altogether for our sakes?" and answering that "he that ploweth should plow in hope." If the apostles have "sown unto you spiritual things," it is no great matter to "reap your carnal things." He argues finally from the sanctuary — "they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar" — and from the Lord's own command: "Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel." Then the whole structure is renounced in a sentence: "Nevertheless we have not used this power; but suffer all things, lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ." Preaching itself earns him nothing to boast in, "for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!" His only wage is to have no wage — "that, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge, that I abuse not my power in the gospel." From this renunciation flows the chapter's most quoted principle: "though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more." To the Jews he became as a Jew, to those under the law as under the law, "To them that are without law, as without law, (being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ,)" and "To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." The chapter closes in the stadium. "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain." Every competitor "is temperate in all things" for "a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible." So Paul runs "not as uncertainly" and fights "not as one that beateth the air," and ends with a warning aimed squarely at himself: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway."
takeaways: Paul spends fourteen verses proving a right he has no intention of using, and the length of the proof is the point. Nature says the soldier does not fund his own campaign and "who planteth a vineyard, and eateth not of the fruit thereof?"; the law says "Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treadeth out the corn"; the sanctuary says "they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar"; and above all "the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel." Only after the right is raised as high as it can go does he set it down — "Nevertheless we have not used this power." A surrender is worth nothing if the thing surrendered was never really owned, so Paul establishes ownership first and then gives it away.

The criterion that governs the renunciation is not personal preference but effect on others: he suffers all things "lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ." This is the same test he had just applied to meat offered to idols, now turned inward, and it reframes the whole question of Christian liberty. The relevant question is never merely whether an act is permitted, since Paul concedes at every step that support is permitted and even commanded, but whether insisting on the permission would put weight on the gospel that someone else has to carry. A right that becomes an obstacle to another's salvation is a right worth losing.

Preaching gives Paul no ground for pride because it was never his idea. "For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel!" He distinguishes between doing the work "willingly," for which there is a reward, and doing it "against my will," in which case "a dispensation of the gospel is committed unto me" regardless — the commission holds either way, but only the free embrace of it is crowned. A calling is not an accomplishment; the most one can do with a debt is to pay it gladly, and Paul's chosen way of paying gladly is to refuse payment.

"I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some" has a fixed center that the slogan usually loses. Paul bends on custom — Jewish observance among Jews, freedom from it among Gentiles, weakness among the weak — but immediately guards the boundary in the same breath: he is "without law" only in the sense of not being under the Mosaic code, "being not without law to God, but under the law to Christ." Accommodation reaches as far as culture and no further; it is a strategy for entering another person's world, not a licence to leave Christ's. And the aim is stated with sober modesty — not to win everyone but "by all means save some."

The direction of the movement is always downward. Paul is "free from all men" and makes himself "servant unto all"; he does not summon the weak to rise to his level of knowledge but goes down to theirs — "To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak." Where the Corinthians used their strength as a platform, Paul spends his on descent. The pattern is the one he has been urging on them all along: the strong exist for the weak, and knowledge is measured by whether it can stoop.

The chapter ends with an apostle warning himself. The images are athletic and unsentimental — a race in which "one receiveth the prize," a discipline in which "every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things," a fight that is not shadowboxing, "not as one that beateth the air." Paul's bodily discipline is not contempt for the body but training of it: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection." And the stated reason is the possibility of personal loss — "lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway." Preaching to others is no guarantee for the preacher; the crown is "incorruptible," but it is still run for.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 25:4 — Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn
crossRefs.why: Paul lifts this single line out of a chapter of civil ordinances and asks "Doth God take care for oxen? Or saith he it altogether for our sakes?" The move shows how he reads the law: a humane rule about a working animal carries a principle about all who labour, so that the ox threshing with its mouth free becomes the pattern for the preacher who lives of the gospel.

crossRefs.label: Luke 10:7 — the labourer is worthy of his hire
crossRefs.why: When Paul says "the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel," this is the ordinance he means. Christ sends out the seventy with instructions to accept food and lodging from those they serve, which makes support of preachers a dominical command rather than a Pauline convenience — and makes Paul's refusal of it a free renunciation of something Christ Himself granted.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 5:17-18 — Thou shalt not muzzle the ox... The labourer is worthy of his reward
crossRefs.why: The same two texts Paul joins here reappear together as the basis for honouring "the elders that rule well... especially they who labour in the word and doctrine." The pairing shows that the argument of this chapter was not a one-off self-defence but became settled teaching on the material support of ministers, even though Paul personally declined it at Corinth.

crossRefs.label: Acts 20:33-35 — these hands have ministered unto my necessities
crossRefs.why: Paul's farewell at Miletus is the same policy stated in his own voice years later: "I have coveted no man's silver, or gold, or apparel," and manual labour supported both him and his companions. It confirms that "we have not used this power" describes a sustained practice, and it supplies the motive — "so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive."

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 11:7-9 — I have preached to you the gospel of God freely
crossRefs.why: The later letter shows the cost and the controversy of the policy defended here. Paul asks whether he "committed an offence in abasing myself that ye might be exalted," admits "I robbed other churches, taking wages of them, to do you service," and insists he was "chargeable to no man" at Corinth. Reading the two together explains why chapter 9 sounds defensive: his refusal of support was being used against him as evidence that he was no true apostle.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 3:12-14 — I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling
crossRefs.why: The runner of this chapter appears again, and again in the first person: "Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after." Both passages place a mature apostle in mid-course rather than at the finish, which is why the warning about becoming "a castaway" is not false modesty but the same settled self-understanding.

interpretationNotes.claim: On the "power to lead about a sister, a wife, as well as other apostles, and as the brethren of the Lord, and Cephas," Catholic reading grants readily that some apostles were married men, since the Gospels show Peter with a mother-in-law, and reads the verse as being about a right of support rather than about the marriage bond as such: the community owed maintenance to an apostle and to the believing woman travelling with him. On this reading the whole chapter is the charter for freely chosen renunciation in ministry. Paul possesses the right, proves it at length, and then declines it, exactly as he declines wages, so that nothing may "hinder the gospel of Christ" — and this is precisely the logic by which the Latin Church came to ask celibacy of her clergy. Celibacy is presented not as a denial that the apostles had the right, but as the disciplined embrace of the very freedom Paul models here and commends in the preceding chapter on the unmarried who care "for the things that belong to the Lord."

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings take the verse as straightforward evidence that married apostles travelled with their wives at the churches' expense, and therefore as evidence against any rule that bars married men from ministry. If Peter and "the brethren of the Lord" led wives about with apostolic sanction, then the ordinary state of a minister may be marriage, and a later requirement of celibacy imposes as law what Paul here treats as one option among several. They add that Paul's own celibacy is consistently presented by him as a personal gift and a strategic freedom rather than a condition of office. Both traditions agree on the substance of what Paul is doing in the chapter: he is renouncing a genuine right, and voluntary self-denial for the gospel's sake is honourable in a way that compelled self-denial is not.

interpretationNotes.claim: The phrase "the brethren of the Lord" is understood in Catholic reading as designating a wider circle of kinsmen — cousins or other close relatives of Jesus — rather than further children of Mary. The supporting considerations offered are that the biblical vocabulary for brother regularly covers extended kinship, that the men named elsewhere as the Lord's brethren are identified as sons of another Mary, and that from the cross Jesus commits His mother to a disciple rather than to a brother, which would be strange if she had other sons. Read this way, the verse names a group of relatives who became notable missionaries in the early Church, and it leaves untouched the belief in Mary's perpetual virginity.

counterpoint.summary: Most Protestant readings take "the brethren of the Lord" in its ordinary sense as sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus, noting that the Gospels list brothers and sisters alongside His mother in a way that reads naturally as one household, and that nothing in the text signals an extended-family usage. On this view the perpetual virginity of Mary is a later development that the plain sense of passages like this one does not support and in places resists. A minority of Protestants, especially in the older confessional streams, have retained belief in Mary's perpetual virginity and read the term as Catholics do. Both traditions agree that the men in question were close relatives of Jesus, that they were not among the Twelve, and that at least one of them became a leader of the Jerusalem church.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes the closing athletic passage at full weight on both halves: the crown is real and the loss is real. "So run, that ye may obtain" and "we an incorruptible" crown are read as genuine promises of reward for a life run well, and the tradition speaks of merit precisely here — not as a wage extracted from God by unaided effort, but as the reward God has freely bound Himself to give to works done in and by His grace. Correspondingly, "lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" is read as a real possibility of final loss for a baptized and even apostolic man. Grace received can be forfeited by grave sin; hence the ascetical language of keeping the body under and bringing it into subjection, and hence the Church's insistence that the assurance proper to a Christian is confident hope rather than certainty of one's own final perseverance.

counterpoint.summary: Protestants are divided here, and the division is old. Those who hold to the perseverance of the saints argue that the elect cannot finally be lost and that warnings like this one are among the ordinary means by which God actually keeps them — the warning is heeded, and the heeding is itself grace; some in this stream also take "castaway" as disqualification from the race or loss of reward rather than damnation. Those who hold that grace may be finally resisted read the verse much as Catholics do, as evidence that even an apostle could fall away, and see in it a standing argument against unconditional security. On the crown, Protestants broadly resist the language of merit, preferring to say that God graciously rewards works He Himself produces, so that the reward is real but never earned. Both traditions agree that the warning is addressed to believers, that it is meant to be taken seriously rather than explained away, and that Christian life is a disciplined race with an outcome that matters.

verses.text: Moreover, brethren, I would not that ye should be ignorant, how that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea;
And were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea;
And did all eat the same spiritual meat;
And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.
But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted.
Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them; as it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.
Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand.
Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed of serpents.
Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer.
Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.

There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.
Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry.
I speak as to wise men; judge ye what I say.
The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread.
Behold Israel after the flesh: are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar?
What say I then? that the idol is any thing, or that which is offered in sacrifice to idols is any thing?
But I say, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God: and I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils.
Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord’s table, and of the table of devils.
Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? are we stronger than he?
All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not.
Let no man seek his own, but every man another’s wealth.
Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake:
For the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof.
If any of them that believe not bid you to a feast, and ye be disposed to go; whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake.
But if any man say unto you, This is offered in sacrifice unto idols, eat not for his sake that shewed it, and for conscience sake: for the earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof:
Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the other: for why is my liberty judged of another man’s conscience?
For if I by grace be a partaker, why am I evil spoken of for that for which I give thanks?
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God:
Even as I please all men in all things, not seeking mine own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved.

chapters.summary: Paul has just warned that even he could become "a castaway," and he now proves the point from Israel's history. "Moreover, brethren, I would not that ye should be ignorant, how that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; And were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea; And did all eat the same spiritual meat; And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ." Five times he says "all" — every one of them had the sign, the food, the drink, the Rock — and then the hinge: "But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness." The wilderness generation becomes a mirror. "Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted." Four failures follow in order: idolatry, quoted straight from the golden calf — "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play"; fornication, where "some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand"; tempting Christ, where they "were destroyed of serpents"; and murmuring, where they "were destroyed of the destroyer." All of it "happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come." The application is aimed at Corinthian confidence: "Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall." Yet the warning is immediately cushioned by a promise — "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it." From this comes the command the whole chapter has been building toward: "Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry." Then, addressing them as adults — "I speak as to wise men; judge ye what I say" — Paul explains why eating at a pagan shrine is not a neutral act. He does it by pointing at their own table: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread." Israel's worshippers who "eat of the sacrifices" are "partakers of the altar," and the same logic runs the other way: though "the idol is" nothing, "the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God," and Paul will not have them "have fellowship with devils." Hence the flat impossibility: "Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils. Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? are we stronger than he?" Having closed the shrine, Paul reopens the marketplace. The Corinthian slogan returns with two qualifications — "All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not" — followed by the rule that governs the rest: "Let no man seek his own, but every man another's wealth." So: "Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake: For the earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof." Accept a pagan's dinner invitation and eat what is served, no questions asked. But if someone points it out — "This is offered in sacrifice unto idols" — then abstain, and Paul is precise about whose scruple governs: "Conscience, I say, not thine own, but of the other." The chapter ends by lifting the whole squabble about menus into doxology and mission: "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God. Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God: Even as I please all men in all things, not seeking mine own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved."
takeaways: The fivefold "all" of the opening verses is the argument in miniature. Every Israelite was "under the cloud," "passed through the sea," was "baptized unto Moses," ate "the same spiritual meat" and drank "the same spiritual drink" — and "with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness." Paul is dismantling a specific Corinthian assumption: that having received the signs guarantees the destination. Sharing in the gifts is not the same as arriving, and the gifts themselves become the measure by which the recipients are judged. What makes the history binding rather than merely instructive is the identification at its centre: "that Rock was Christ." Paul does not say Israel had a shadow while the Church has the substance; he says the same Christ was already feeding and watering them in the desert, which is why he can call their food and drink "spiritual" without irony and still record that they died. If they perished with Christ present among them, no Corinthian can treat presence as immunity, and "let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" follows with force.

Between the warning and the command Paul plants a promise that keeps the warning from becoming despair: "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape." Three things are asserted at once — that no Corinthian trial is unprecedented, that the limit on temptation is set by God's faithfulness rather than by our strength, and that the escape is provided along with the trial rather than instead of it. The stated purpose is not the removal of pressure but the capacity "to bear it." And the escape offered in this very chapter is blunt and physical: "flee from idolatry."

Paul answers the question of idol-food not with a theory of matter but with a theology of the table. "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" Eating together at a sacred table joins the eater to what is on it and to everyone else eating — "we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread." That is why Israel's worshippers are "partakers of the altar" and why a shrine banquet cannot be a private matter of digestion. Paul grants that "the idol is" nothing and still forbids the meal, because what stands behind the nothing is not nothing: "the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils."

"Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils" is a statement of impossibility, not merely a prohibition. The Corinthians presumably could and did do both, so Paul is saying the two acts cancel each other — one cannot belong to two tables any more than a spouse can belong to two marriages, which is why he reaches for the language of divine jealousy: "Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? are we stronger than he?" The rhetorical question exposes the real absurdity of their confidence. Enlightened liberty was never strong enough for the contest it had wandered into, and the only sane response to a rival claim on one's allegiance is the one already given: "flee."

Having drawn one hard line, Paul refuses to draw a hundred soft ones. "Whatsoever is sold in the shambles, that eat, asking no question for conscience sake: For the earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof." Meat in the market is God's before it is anyone's, and scrupulous investigation is itself a failure of faith. The single limit is another person: if a man identifies the food as sacrificial, abstain — "not thine own, but of the other" conscience — because the meal has now become a statement he will read. Liberty is real, and it is spent, not hoarded, which is exactly what "Let no man seek his own, but every man another's wealth" means in practice.

The chapter's conclusion refuses to leave the matter at the level of etiquette. "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" makes the most ordinary act liturgical, and "Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God" names three audiences at once — the synagogue, the pagan neighbour, and the congregation. Paul's own standard is the missionary one he has just described in his own case: "not seeking mine own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved." The final measure of a disputed freedom is whether anyone was saved by how it was used.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 17:6 — thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it
crossRefs.why: This is the event behind "they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ." The narrative supplies the water and the murmuring at Massah; Paul supplies the identification. Reading them together shows how he handles the wilderness story — not as an illustration borrowed for a sermon, but as an episode in which Christ was already present and already the source of Israel's life.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 32:6 — the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play
crossRefs.why: Paul quotes this line verbatim as his definition of idolatry, and the choice of quotation is deliberate: he picks not the moment the calf was cast but the moment the people held a feast in front of it. The golden calf was, precisely, a meal at a shrine — which is exactly the practice the Corinthians were defending — and it took place immediately after the covenant had been ratified, by people who had every sign God had given.

crossRefs.label: Numbers 25 — the people did eat, and bowed down to their gods
crossRefs.why: The episode at Baal-peor is Paul's example of fornication, and it fuses the two sins he treats in this letter: Israel joins in the sacrificial meals of Moab and then in immorality with Moabite women, so that the shared table and the shared bed are one apostasy. The numbers differ between the accounts — Paul writes "three and twenty thousand" where Numbers records twenty-four thousand — a discrepancy readers have long noted and variously explained; his point rests on the event, not the tally.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 32:16-17 — They sacrificed unto devils, not to God... They provoked him to jealousy
crossRefs.why: Both halves of Paul's argument are already here. The claim that pagan sacrifice terminates in devils rather than in the gods it names, and the response of divine jealousy that Paul invokes with "Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?", are drawn from the Song of Moses. The allusion also carries its own context: this is the song given to Israel as a witness against them for the very failures Paul has just listed.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 24:1 — The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof
crossRefs.why: Paul quotes this twice in nine verses, and it does the liberating work in the chapter. If everything already belongs to God, then no pagan rite can transfer ownership of a piece of meat, and interrogating the butcher is unnecessary. The same psalm goes on to ask who may ascend the hill of the Lord and answers with clean hands and a pure heart, which is the balance Paul keeps: the creation is free to use, and the worshipper is still accountable.

crossRefs.label: John 6:51-56 — Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you
crossRefs.why: The discourse on the bread of life is the closest Gospel parallel to "the communion of the body of Christ," and it shares this chapter's framing: Jesus contrasts the manna Israel ate in the wilderness, after which "your fathers did eat manna... and are dead," with the bread that gives life. Paul makes the same comparison with the same conclusion, that the wilderness food did not save those who ate it, and both passages have long been the ground on which readings of the Eucharist are argued.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes the opening typology as a genuine sacramental parallel: the cloud and the sea prefigure baptism, the manna and the water from the rock prefigure the Eucharist, and Paul's whole warning depends on the correspondence being real. From this the tradition draws two conclusions it holds together. First, the sacraments truly give what they signify — the fathers really were "baptized unto Moses" and really did eat "spiritual meat," and Christ really was the Rock — so these are not bare emblems. Second, and just as strongly, the sacraments do not work as charms: those who received them all were nonetheless "overthrown in the wilderness," which is why the Church insists that a sacrament must be received with living faith and repentance, and why grave sin after baptism is a real danger requiring real remedy. The verse "let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" is read as excluding presumption about one's own final salvation.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters agree that the passage is typological and that it is a warning against sacramental presumption — indeed many read it as the New Testament's sharpest argument against supposing that rites confer grace by their performance. The disagreement is over what conclusion follows. Reformed readings take the chapter as evidence that outward participation in the covenant community never guaranteed salvation, distinguishing the visible church from the elect and treating the wilderness generation as those who had the signs without the thing signified; the warning is genuine and is one means by which God preserves His own. Memorialist readings go further and take the parallel to show that the ordinances are signs of a grace already received by faith, not channels of it. Those Protestants who hold that grace can be finally lost read the passage much as Catholics do. All agree that Paul's practical instruction is identical on either account: "flee from idolatry."

interpretationNotes.claim: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" is, in Catholic reading, among the plainest New Testament statements of the real presence. The argument turns on it: Paul is explaining why one cannot eat at a shrine, and the explanation only works if eating at the Lord's table joins the communicant to Christ as objectively as eating at a pagan table joins the eater to what is sacrificed there. The words are read at face value — what is shared is the blood and the body, not a symbol of them — and the phrase "which we bless" is understood to name an action performed over the cup, a consecration by the Church, rather than mere thanksgiving before a meal. The next verse then draws the ecclesial consequence: "we being many are one bread, and one body," so that the sacrament both presupposes and creates the unity of the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings range widely and the range matters. Sacramental Protestants hold that Christ is truly given and received in the Supper, so that the participation Paul describes is real communion with the crucified Christ, while declining the account of how the elements are changed. Reformed readings emphasize that the word rendered "communion" means sharing or participation, and that believers are genuinely made partakers of Christ by the Spirit in the act of receiving, though the body remains where the ascended Christ is; the sharing is real and spiritual rather than local. Memorialist readings take the participation to be fellowship in the benefits of Christ's death and in the body of believers, pointing to the next verse's "one bread, and one body" as evidence that Paul's concern is corporate belonging. All these readings agree with the Catholic one on the argument's structure: the Supper creates a binding allegiance, which is exactly why it cannot be combined with the table of devils.

interpretationNotes.claim: In Catholic reading, the three-way comparison Paul draws — the Lord's table, Israel's altar, and "the table of devils" — implies that the Christian table is itself an altar and that what happens there is sacrificial. Paul asks, "Behold Israel after the flesh: are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar?" and applies the same category on both sides of it; the middle term of the comparison is sacrifice, and a comparison between two sacrificial meals and a merely commemorative one would break down. On this reading the Eucharist is the making-present of the one sacrifice of Calvary rather than a new or additional offering, which is why the Church can call it a sacrifice without implying that Christ suffers again, and why the language of altar, table, and partaking sits together naturally in this passage.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters answer that Paul's point of comparison is not sacrifice but fellowship and allegiance. What the three tables share is that eating at any of them declares whose you are and binds you to that company; the argument works on that basis alone and does not require the Supper to be an offering. They urge that the New Testament writers avoid calling the Christian assembly's table an altar in the sacrificial sense, and that the letter to the Hebrews insists on a single offering made once and never repeated, so that a continuing sacrifice would obscure the finished work it proclaims. In their reading the Supper shows forth a sacrifice rather than performing one. Both traditions affirm that the death of Christ is unrepeatable and sufficient, that the Supper is inseparably tied to it, and that partaking makes a public declaration of allegiance that cannot be doubled.

verses.text: Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.
Now I praise you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you.
But I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.
Every man praying or prophesying, having his head covered, dishonoureth his head.
But every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven.
For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered.
For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, forasmuch as he is the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man.
For the man is not of the woman; but the woman of the man.
Neither was the man created for the woman; but the woman for the man.
For this cause ought the woman to have power on her head because of the angels.
Nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord.
For as the woman is of the man, even so is the man also by the woman; but all things of God.
Judge in yourselves: is it comely that a woman pray unto God uncovered?
Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him?
But if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering.
But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God.
Now in this that I declare unto you I praise you not, that ye come together not for the better, but for the worse.
For first of all, when ye come together in the church, I hear that there be divisions among you; and I partly believe it.
For there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you.
When ye come together therefore into one place, this is not to eat the Lord’s supper.
For in eating every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken.
What? have ye not houses to eat and to drink in? or despise ye the church of God, and shame them that have not? What shall I say to you? shall I praise you in this? I praise you not.
For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread:
And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come.
Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.
For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep.
For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.
But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world.
Wherefore, my brethren, when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another.
And if any man hunger, let him eat at home; that ye come not together unto condemnation. And the rest will I set in order when I come.

chapters.summary: "Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ" closes the long argument about liberty and opens a new one about assembly. Paul begins with praise — "I praise you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you" — and then takes up the first of two things that go wrong when the Corinthians gather. The first is a matter of dress and of order. "I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God." From this comes the rule: a man who prays or prophesies "having his head covered, dishonoureth his head," while "every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven." Paul reasons from creation — the man "is the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man," since "the man is not of the woman; but the woman of the man" — and adds the odd, unexplained clause that the woman ought "to have power on her head because of the angels." Then, having drawn the asymmetry, he immediately refuses to let it become independence: "Nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as the woman is of the man, even so is the man also by the woman; but all things of God." He appeals to their own judgment and to what "nature itself" teaches about long hair, noting that a woman's hair "is given her for a covering," and closes the section by declining to argue further: "But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God." The second problem draws no praise at all. "Now in this that I declare unto you I praise you not, that ye come together not for the better, but for the worse." There are "divisions among you," which Paul partly believes, and which he says will serve to show "they which are approved"; but the result is that "when ye come together therefore into one place, this is not to eat the Lord's supper." Each brings his own food and eats it first, "and one is hungry, and another is drunken" — a supper that reproduces the class divisions of the city inside the church. Paul's rebuke is scalding: "have ye not houses to eat and to drink in? or despise ye the church of God, and shame them that have not?" Against this he sets the tradition he received and handed on: "For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me. After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me." The rite is not private and not merely retrospective: "as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come." From this follows the warning: "whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord," so "let a man examine himself, and so let him eat." To eat "unworthily" is to eat "damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body," and Paul says the consequences are already visible: "For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep." Yet even this judgment is fatherly — "when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" — and the practical remedy is almost disappointingly plain: "when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another. And if any man hunger, let him eat at home; that ye come not together unto condemnation. And the rest will I set in order when I come."
takeaways: Paul frames both halves of this chapter as handed-down tradition rather than personal opinion. He praises them for keeping "the ordinances, as I delivered them to you," and introduces the Supper with the formula "I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you." The verbs are those of careful transmission, and they place the words of institution among the earliest Christian material we possess — written down years before any Gospel, describing what happened "the same night in which he was betrayed." Whatever a reader concludes about the practices at issue, Paul is not inventing them; he is passing on a deposit and correcting a church that has drifted from it.

The head-covering argument is easy to caricature and harder to read carefully, because Paul builds the asymmetry and then blocks its abuse in the same breath. He does say "the head of the woman is the man"; he also says "the head of Christ is God," which puts headship inside the life of God rather than in the category of superiority and inferiority. He argues from the order of creation, and then adds "Nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as the woman is of the man, even so is the man also by the woman; but all things of God." And the whole passage assumes without comment that women pray and prophesy aloud in the assembly — the question at issue is how, not whether.

The way the section ends is as instructive as its content. After appeals to creation, to the angels, to nature, and to their own judgment, Paul finishes with "if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God." He is willing to state a practice, give reasons for it, and then decline to fight about it, resting the case on the settled usage of the churches rather than on further argument. Contentiousness is treated as the real disorder; a man determined to quarrel about head coverings has already lost the point of the assembly he is quarrelling in.

The Corinthian abuse of the Supper is not doctrinal error but social contempt, and Paul treats the two as inseparable. "In eating every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken" — the wealthy eat their provisions while the poor, arriving late from work, get nothing. Paul's verdict is that this cancels the sacrament: "this is not to eat the Lord's supper." The identical words and elements, used in a gathering that shames "them that have not," do not produce the Lord's supper at all. A rite that divides the body while claiming to be the body has become its own contradiction, which is why the remedy is as concrete as the sin: "tarry one for another."

"Ye do shew the Lord's death till he come" gives the rite three tenses at once. It reaches back to a night that can be dated and named; it does something in the present, since to "shew" is to proclaim publicly rather than to recall privately; and it is bounded by a future — "till he come" — so that every celebration is provisional and points past itself. Remembrance in this sense is not nostalgia for an absent friend but the Church's standing public announcement of a death, made by eating and drinking, and made repeatedly "as often as" she gathers.

The warnings in the final verses assume that something more than bread is at stake. To eat "unworthily" is not to be insufficiently holy — no one would ever eat on those terms — but to eat in the manner Paul has just described, and the charge is startlingly severe: such a person is "guilty of the body and blood of the Lord." The prescribed response is self-examination rather than abstention: "let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread." The diagnosis is failure at "discerning the Lord's body," and even the resulting sickness and death among them are read as correction rather than condemnation — "when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world." Judgment inside the Church is presented as mercy at work.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 2:22-23 — she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man
crossRefs.why: Paul's premises in verses 8 and 9 are lifted directly from this narrative: "the man is not of the woman; but the woman of the man," and "neither was the man created for the woman; but the woman for the man." The source passage also supplies the counterweight he adds in verse 11, since the woman is made because "it is not good that the man should be alone" and is greeted as "bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" — mutual belonging, not mere derivation.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 3:28 — there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus
crossRefs.why: The sharpest internal tension in reading this chapter is between the created-order argument here and the baptismal declaration there, and both are Paul's. His own bridge is verse 11, "neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord," where the phrase "in the Lord" does the same work as "in Christ Jesus" does in Galatians. How far that oneness reshapes the ordering described here is precisely where interpreters divide.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 12:14 — this day shall be unto you for a memorial... by an ordinance for ever
crossRefs.why: "This do in remembrance of me" is spoken at a Passover meal, and the Passover was itself commanded as a perpetual memorial in which each generation was to count itself among those brought out of Egypt. Reading the institution against its background shows that biblical remembrance is a liturgical act with present effect rather than a mental exercise, and it explains why Paul can move so quickly from a supper to a covenant: the meal in Exodus was where a delivered people learned who they were.

crossRefs.label: Luke 22:19-20 — This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me
crossRefs.why: Of the Gospel accounts this is the closest to Paul's, sharing both "this do in remembrance of me" and the description of the cup as "the new testament in my blood." The agreement of two independent early witnesses on the same wording indicates a fixed liturgical form already in use, and Luke's setting — "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer" — supplies the context Paul assumes but does not state.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 — is it not the communion of the body of Christ?... we being many are one bread, and one body
crossRefs.why: The previous chapter states the principle this one applies. There Paul argues that sharing the cup and the bread joins the participants to Christ and to each other, "for we are all partakers of that one bread"; here he confronts a church whose manner of eating denies exactly that. The two passages together explain why humiliating the poor at the meal is not a lapse of manners but a failure at "discerning the Lord's body."

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 10:29 — hath counted the blood of the covenant... an unholy thing
crossRefs.why: The same logic of aggravated guilt appears there: contempt shown toward the blood of the covenant is treated as an offence of a different order than ordinary transgression. It illuminates Paul's charge that one who eats unworthily is "guilty of the body and blood of the Lord," and it shares the assumption that severe warnings belong inside the Church, addressed to people already sanctified, rather than to outsiders.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes the head-covering passage as a genuine apostolic tradition — Paul explicitly praises the Corinthians for keeping "the ordinances, as I delivered them to you" — while distinguishing within it between an abiding principle and a disciplinary form. The abiding element is the created order Paul argues from, the differentiation of man and woman as willed by God and as bearing meaning in worship, together with the reverence and modesty proper to the assembly. The form, a veil on the head, is a custom the Church has authority to require, adapt, or relax, and in fact veiling was general church practice for many centuries before being left free in modern times. This is offered as an ordinary example of how the Church handles a scriptural directive: the apostolic principle is preserved, while the concrete discipline that expresses it is governed by the living authority of the Church, which is also how Paul himself concludes the matter, by appealing to the settled usage of "the churches of God" rather than to further argument. On "the head of the woman is the man," the tradition reads headship in light of "the head of Christ is God," that is, as an order of relation within an equality of nature, not a difference of dignity.

counterpoint.summary: Protestants divide, and the division does not track the usual lines. One reading holds that Paul grounds the practice in creation, angels, and nature rather than in local custom, and that the covering therefore remains binding wherever the passage is obeyed; a minority of congregations still practice it. A far more common reading holds that the covering was a first-century cultural signal of respectability whose meaning has not survived, so that obeying Paul today means honouring the principle of orderly, non-provocative, reverent worship in whatever the local equivalent may be — and points out that Paul himself appeals to "nature" and to their own judgment, arguments that assume shared cultural intuitions. Both readings resist the idea that an ecclesiastical authority may bind or loose the practice on its own authority, holding instead that the text's own distinction between principle and form must be discerned from Scripture. Egalitarian and complementarian Protestants further divide over "the head of the woman is the man," the first pressing verses 11-12 and the fact that women here pray and prophesy publicly, the second pressing verses 3-9 as a permanent ordering of roles. All agree the passage assumes women's audible participation in worship.

interpretationNotes.claim: On the words of institution, Catholic reading takes "this is my body, which is broken for you" and "This cup is the new testament in my blood" in their plain sense: what is given is Christ Himself under the forms of bread and wine. "This do in remembrance of me" is read as a command that constitutes an office as well as a rite — a charge given to the apostles to do what He did — and the remembrance it commands is understood in the biblical sense of memorial, in which a past saving act is made present to those who keep it, as the Passover made the exodus present to every generation. Hence the Church's teaching that the Eucharist does not repeat Calvary but makes the one sacrifice present; "ye do shew the Lord's death till he come" is read as a proclamation that does what it says. The tradition also draws from this passage the practice of receiving with reverence and preparation, and from Paul's careful language of receiving and delivering, the conviction that the liturgy is something handed on rather than devised.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings again span a range. Sacramental Protestants hold that Christ truly gives Himself to the faithful receiver in the Supper, so that the words are not empty, while declining any account of a change in the elements. Reformed readings emphasize that believers are lifted by the Spirit to feed on Christ, who remains the ascended Lord; the presence is real but not local, and "till he come" is taken to imply that He is bodily absent in the interim. Memorialist readings take "in remembrance of me" as its own explanation and read the Supper as a solemn, covenantal act of remembering and proclaiming. Common Protestant textual observations are that Paul continues to call the element "this bread" after the institution, and that a memorial and a sacrifice are different categories. Both traditions agree that the Supper was instituted by Christ, that its words come with dominical authority, that it proclaims His death publicly, and that it looks forward to His return.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord" as evidence for the objective reality of what is received: one cannot be guilty of a body and blood that are not there. Correspondingly "not discerning the Lord's body" is read primarily as a failure to recognize what the sacrament is. From this the Church derives a real discipline — that grave sin should be repented and, where it is mortal, sacramentally confessed before receiving; that the community may and must regulate admission to communion; and that the fitting posture toward the sacrament is reverence and preparation rather than casual approach. The bodily consequences Paul reports, that "many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep," are taken at face value as chastisement, and read together with "we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" as a picture of purifying discipline within the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take "not discerning the Lord's body" in light of the abuse that occasioned the whole passage, and understand the body being failed as the Church — the poor who are shamed are the body of Christ that the Corinthians are not recognizing. Read this way, the sin Paul condemns is not irreverence toward the elements but contempt for the gathered people, which is why his remedy is "tarry one for another" rather than any change in the rite. On worthiness, they emphasize that Paul's instruction is to examine and then eat, not to examine and then abstain, and that the qualification for the table is faith and repentance rather than absolution granted through a priest; the Supper is given to sinners who know themselves such. Many Protestant traditions nonetheless practise a form of fencing the table and call for self-examination and reconciliation beforehand, and some read the passage as Catholics do, taking reverence toward the sacrament itself to be at issue. Both traditions agree that the warning is real, that the Supper is not to be approached carelessly, and that Paul's judgment language is corrective and aimed at saving rather than destroying.

verses.text: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant.
Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led.
Wherefore I give you to understand, that no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost.
Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit.
And there are differences of administrations, but the same Lord.
And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all.
But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.
For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit;
To another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit;
To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues:
But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.
For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ.
For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit.
For the body is not one member, but many.
If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?
And if the ear shall say, Because I am not the eye, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?
If the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing? If the whole were hearing, where were the smelling?
But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him.
And if they were all one member, where were the body?
But now are they many members, yet but one body.
And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you.
Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary:
And those members of the body, which we think to be less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour; and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness.
For our comely parts have no need: but God hath tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked:
That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another.
And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it.
Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular.
And God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues.
Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers? are all workers of miracles?
Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?
But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way.

chapters.summary: Paul opens a new section with the formula he reserves for contested matters: "Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant." He begins by reminding the Corinthians what they were before, "Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led" — a religious past of mute images and unaccountable seizure — and he hands them a first test for any inspired speech: "no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost." Confession, not intensity, marks the Spirit. From that test he lays down the pattern that governs everything after it, a triple refrain that traces variety back to a single source: "there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit," "differences of administrations, but the same Lord," "diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all." The purpose clause matters as much as the refrain, since "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal." A list follows — "the word of wisdom," "the word of knowledge," "faith," "the gifts of healing," "the working of miracles," "prophecy," "discerning of spirits," "divers kinds of tongues," "the interpretation of tongues" — and every item is closed off from boasting by the same clause: all are worked by "that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will." Then comes the image that carries the remainder of the chapter: "For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ." Membership is not achieved but conferred, for "by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit." Paul then works the metaphor from both ends. Against the member who counts himself excluded he sets the foot and the ear: "If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body; is it therefore not of the body?" Against the member who counts himself sufficient he sets the eye and the head: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you." The arrangement belongs to God, for "now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him," and that arrangement reverses the ranking men would make, since "those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary" and God has "tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked." The aim is stated without disguise: "That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another," issuing in a shared nervous system where "whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it." The application lands directly on them — "Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular" — and Paul names an ordered arrangement that "God hath set... in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers, after that miracles, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, diversities of tongues." A run of questions expecting the answer no — "Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers?... do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?" — forecloses the idea that any one gift is the mark of the Spirit's presence. The chapter ends by permitting ambition and redirecting it: "covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way."
takeaways: The chapter's opening test is doctrinal rather than experiential. Corinth had come out of a world of "dumb idols" whose worshippers were "carried away... even as ye were led," where the mark of the divine was being overtaken by a power that could not speak. Paul refuses to let that be the standard of Christian inspiration and substitutes a confession: "no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost." The Spirit's signature is articulate and christological, which means an experience is not self-authenticating simply because it is overwhelming, and a plain confession of the lordship of Jesus is already the Spirit's work in a person who has never spoken in tongues.

The threefold refrain — "the same Spirit," "the same Lord," "the same God which worketh all in all" — makes diversity an argument for unity rather than against it. Paul does not flatten the gifts into sameness; he shows that their variety is itself evidence of a single giver, which strips the recipient of any ground for pride, since "all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will." Nothing on the list was earned, chosen, or deserved, so nothing on the list can be a credential.

The purpose clause governs everything: "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal." A gift is not a possession but an assignment, given to one person for the benefit of others, which reverses the direction Corinth had been reading it in. This is also the standard by which Paul will later rank prophecy above uninterpreted tongues, and it means the question to ask of any spiritual endowment is not what it proves about its bearer but what good it does the assembly.

The body image is aimed at two opposite failures at once. The foot who says "Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body" and the eye who says to the hand "I have no need of thee" commit the same error from opposite ends: both treat their own function as the measure of belonging. Paul's answer to each is the same fact — "now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him" — so that self-exclusion and self-sufficiency are both refusals of God's own arrangement.

God's ordering deliberately inverts visible prestige, since "those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary," and God has "tempered the body together, having given more abundant honour to that part which lacked." The stated goal is negative and positive together: "That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another." The result is a body with a shared nervous system, where "whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it," so indifference to another Christian's suffering is not merely uncharitable but anatomically impossible for a healthy member.

The closing verses hold two things together that are often set against each other. Structure is divine — "God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers" — and the ordinal words indicate that the gifts are not interchangeable in value. Yet the questions "Are all apostles? are all prophets?... do all speak with tongues?" rule out any single gift as the universal proof of the Spirit. Ambition is not condemned but reoriented: "covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way," so the chapter that most exalts the charisms ends by subordinating all of them to something else.

crossRefs.label: Romans 12:4-6 — as we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office
crossRefs.why: Paul makes the same argument to a church he had never visited, and the overlap shows the body image is not an ad hoc rebuke of Corinth but his settled account of the Church. There the practical fruit is stated first — "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think" — and the gifts are held "according to the grace that is given to us," which supplies the humility that 1 Corinthians 12 argues toward.

crossRefs.label: Ephesians 4:4-16 — There is one body, and one Spirit... he gave some, apostles
crossRefs.why: The unity refrain "one body, and one Spirit... One Lord, one faith, one baptism" restates the triple "same Spirit... same Lord... same God" of this chapter, and the list of those Christ "gave" parallels what "God hath set... in the church." Ephesians adds the goal explicitly — the ministries exist "for the perfecting of the saints" until "the whole body fitly joined together... maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love" — which is the same criterion of profit and edification Paul is applying at Corinth.

crossRefs.label: Acts 2:4-11 — began to speak with other tongues... every man heard them speak in his own language
crossRefs.why: Pentecost supplies the church's founding instance of the gifts Paul is regulating, and the difference is instructive: there the tongues were immediately understood, since "every man heard them speak in his own language," whereas at Corinth an uninterpreted tongue leaves the hearer outside. Reading them together frames the question Paul takes up next, of whether a gift is functioning as sign and communication or only as private experience.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 115:4-8 — They have mouths, but they speak not... They that make them are like unto them
crossRefs.why: Paul's phrase "dumb idols" is not a throwaway insult but a deliberate contrast. The psalm's mockery of images that cannot speak, see, hear, or handle ends with the warning that "they that make them are like unto them," which is exactly the fate Paul says the Corinthians were rescued from when they were "carried away... even as ye were led." The Spirit who now makes them confess "Jesus is the Lord" is the opposite of the speechless gods that once directed them.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 — we being many are one bread, and one body
crossRefs.why: Two chapters earlier Paul had already grounded the oneness of the body in a shared meal: "The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread." That statement stands behind "by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body... and have been all made to drink into one Spirit," tying the body language to what the church actually does when it gathers rather than to metaphor alone.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 1:10-12 — I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas
crossRefs.why: The letter opened with the very disease this chapter diagnoses anatomically. Paul's plea "that there be no divisions among you" is answered here by God's own design of the body "That there should be no schism in the body," and the party slogans of chapter 1 are the social form of the foot saying "I am not of the body" and the eye saying "I have no need of thee."

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers" as describing a structure that is divinely instituted rather than merely convenient. The ordinal words are given weight: the arrangement has a real order, with apostolic office at its head, and the verb is that God "hath set" it in place, so the Church's hierarchical constitution is understood as one of the Spirit's works and not a later human overlay on a formless charismatic community. On this reading the hierarchical gifts and the freely distributed charisms come from the same Spirit and are not rivals, the charisms being ordered to the building up of the one body under the pastors who are charged with discerning them. "Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular" is likewise read of a visible, structured communion, since a body with organs, offices, and mutual dependence is precisely not an invisible aggregate.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings emphasize the sovereign and unpredictable distribution stated in the same passage — the Spirit is "dividing to every man severally as he will" — and read the numbered list as ranking usefulness for edification rather than establishing a chain of jurisdiction. Since "the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man," the whole membership is gifted and the body image is taken to support the common priesthood of all believers, with ordered ministry serving the congregation rather than standing over it. Many hold that apostles and prophets belong to the Church's foundation and are unrepeatable, so the ranked list describes the era in which the gospel was first delivered rather than a permanent office structure; others accept enduring offices but derive their shape from Scripture rather than from an unbroken succession. Both traditions affirm that the ordering is God's own, that no member may opt out or declare another unnecessary, and that gifts exist for the body and not for the holder.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic reading, "by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit" refers to the sacrament actually received. Baptism is not a picture of an incorporation that happens elsewhere; it is the means by which the Spirit joins a person to the visible Body of Christ, which is why the barriers of nation and status are named as abolished in the same breath. The drinking clause is heard alongside the Church's other sacramental life, so that initiation and the shared cup together constitute the one body that Paul then describes organ by organ, and membership in Christ is inseparable from membership in the concrete communion of the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the baptism in view as the Spirit's own act of uniting the believer to Christ, which water baptism signifies and seals rather than accomplishes, and they take the resulting body to be first the whole company of the redeemed rather than a single visible institution. Sacramental Protestants stay close to the Catholic reading in tying sign and thing signified tightly together, while others insist the operative agent in the sentence is the Spirit and the instrument is faith. Pentecostal and charismatic readers add a further distinction, holding that a subsequent baptism in the Holy Spirit empowers for service, while acknowledging that this particular verse describes something universal, since Paul says "we all" without exception. All sides agree that no one joins the body by self-selection, that the divisions of Jew and Gentile, bond and free are dissolved by it, and that the same Spirit is given to every member.
