verses.text: Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.
And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.
Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,
Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;
Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth;
Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.
For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.
But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.
When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.

chapters.summary: This is the "more excellent way" Paul had just promised, and it opens not with a definition but with a series of demolitions in the first person. "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal" — the most exalted speech imaginable reduced to temple noise. He escalates: "though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing," and then moves from endowment to sacrifice, "though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing." Three verdicts descend in order — worthless noise, then nothing, then no profit — so that the whole apparatus of gift, insight, generosity, and even martyrdom is set at zero without the one thing. Only then does Paul describe what charity is, and he does it almost entirely with verbs and mostly by negation: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil; Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth; Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things." Every clause reads like a line drawn against something the Corinthians had actually been doing. The argument then turns to duration, and here Paul makes his decisive point about the gifts they had been competing over: "Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away." The reason is that all present spiritual knowledge is fragmentary — "we know in part, and we prophesy in part" — and fragments are made for a completion that will retire them: "when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away." Two images make this concrete without softening it. The first is growing up: "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things." The second is a metal mirror's imperfect reflection: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known." The chapter ends with a triad and a ranking, and the ranking is the point: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity."
takeaways: The chapter is an argument, not an ornament, and it is bolted to the chapters on either side of it. It answers the promise of chapter twelve, "yet shew I unto you a more excellent way," and is picked up immediately in the next line of chapter fourteen, "Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts." Charity is therefore not offered as an alternative to the gifts but as their measure and their governing habit, which is why Paul can command the pursuit of both in the same sentence. Read out of that setting the passage becomes a wedding poem; read in it, it is the answer to a church tearing itself apart over which endowments matter most.

The opening hypotheticals are all in the first person and all describe things Corinth admired. Angelic speech, prophecy, comprehension of "all mysteries, and all knowledge," mountain-moving faith, total almsgiving, and death by fire are the most impressive religious achievements available, and each is assigned a value of zero without charity. Notice the exact wording of the third verdict: "it profiteth me nothing." Paul had just said the Spirit's manifestations are given "to profit withal," meaning to profit others. A gift can genuinely benefit the church and still leave its bearer with nothing, which is a warning that usefulness and holiness are not the same measurement.

Charity is defined almost entirely by what it will not do. Of the fifteen clauses, most are refusals — "envieth not," "vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up," "Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil," "Rejoiceth not in iniquity." Each of these is a line drawn against something already documented in this letter: the envy behind the party slogans, the puffed-up boasting over teachers and knowledge, the unseemly behaviour at their meals, the self-seeking of those who insisted on their own rights. Paul does not describe charity as a feeling to be summoned but as a set of concrete behaviours to be practised, and he defines it in the vocabulary of their specific failures.

The four "all things" clauses — "Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things" — are not a licence for credulity, because they stand immediately after "Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth." Charity's openness is bounded by truth: it refuses to take pleasure in wrongdoing even when doing so would be convenient, and it refuses to give up on a person even when doing so would be easier. The pairing keeps love from collapsing into either suspicion or sentimentality.

Paul's argument for the supremacy of charity is finally an argument about time. "Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away." The gifts are provisional by design, and the reason given is not that they are defective but that they are partial: "we know in part, and we prophesy in part." To build an identity on a partial thing is to build on something scheduled for retirement. This applies as directly to theological knowledge as to tongues, and it should make anyone holding strong convictions hold them with the humility of a man looking "through a glass, darkly."

The closing triad ranks what abides. Faith, hope, and charity all continue where the charisms do not, but "the greatest of these is charity," and the reason lies in what happens at the consummation Paul has just described. When we see "face to face," faith turns into sight and hope turns into possession, while love has nothing to become because it is already the substance of the end. That makes charity not merely the best Christian behaviour in this life but the shape of eternal life itself, and it explains why a person with every gift and no love is, in Paul's blunt phrase, "nothing."

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 12:31 — covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way
crossRefs.why: This chapter is the promised "more excellent way," and the specific gifts it relativizes are precisely the ones just listed — tongues, prophecy, knowledge, and mountain-moving faith all appear in the preceding catalogue. Reading the two together prevents the common mistake of treating chapter thirteen as a detachable meditation, since its whole force depends on the competitive scramble over charisms that chapter twelve describes.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 14:1 — Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy
crossRefs.why: The next verse resumes the argument without a pause and shows how charity is meant to be applied: it becomes the reason for preferring intelligible prophecy over an uninterpreted tongue, since love seeks the edification of the hearer rather than the satisfaction of the speaker. Chapter thirteen supplies the principle and chapter fourteen the rules that follow from it.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 22:37-40 — On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets
crossRefs.why: Paul's ranking of charity above every gift restates the ranking Jesus gave among the commandments, where love of God and neighbour is the hinge on which everything else turns. The parallel indicates that Paul is not introducing a novel Christian sentiment but applying the Lord's own ordering of the law to a dispute about spiritual endowments.

crossRefs.label: 1 John 4:8,20 — God is love... he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God
crossRefs.why: Where Paul argues that charity outlasts every gift, John supplies the reason by locating love in God's own nature, and he applies the same practical test Paul does: the claim to know God is falsified by failure to love the brother in view. The two passages together keep charity from being read as a merely human virtue or an emotional temperature rather than a participation in what God is.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 5:6,22 — faith which worketh by love... the fruit of the Spirit is love
crossRefs.why: The phrase "faith which worketh by love" bears directly on Paul's claim that "all faith, so that I could remove mountains" is nothing without charity, and it is the passage most often set beside this chapter in debates over how faith and love are related in justification. The listing of love as the first fruit of the Spirit also shows that charity is itself a work of the Spirit and not a human supplement to the Spirit's gifts.

crossRefs.label: Romans 13:10 — Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law
crossRefs.why: Paul's negative definitions here — charity "thinketh no evil" and "seeketh not her own" — are compressed in Romans into the principle that love "worketh no ill to his neighbour." The parallel confirms that the fifteen clauses are not poetic flourishes but a summary of what the commandments require, so that the behaviour described in this chapter is the law's actual content rather than an optional higher path.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds in this chapter the classic statement that faith is not saving unless it is informed by charity. Paul's own words are taken at full strength: "though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing." A person may hold everything true and still be nothing, which is read as showing that charity is not an optional consequence appended to justifying faith but the very form that makes faith living. Faith, hope, and charity are understood as the three theological virtues poured into the soul, and the ranking "the greatest of these is charity" is heard as a statement of dignity and not merely of duration, since charity alone unites the soul directly to God and remains in glory when faith and hope have reached their term. On this reading the growth of the Christian life is measured by growth in charity, and the whole chapter serves as the standard by which any claim of grace, gift, or orthodoxy is finally tested.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters answer first from context: the subject under discussion is the spiritual endowments of chapter twelve, and "all faith, so that I could remove mountains" corresponds to the charism of faith listed there rather than to the trusting reliance on Christ by which a sinner is justified. Paul is not weighing love against saving faith; he is weighing love against the gifts Corinth was competing over. On the standard Protestant account, faith alone is the instrument that receives righteousness precisely because it is an empty hand rather than a virtue, yet faith is never alone in the person who has it, so a loveless faith is by definition a dead and counterfeit faith rather than a real faith lacking a supplement. Charity is called greatest because it endures without alteration into the world to come while faith passes into sight, not because it displaces faith as the means of union with Christ. Both traditions insist that a Christianity without love is worthless, that charity is the Spirit's work and not a human achievement, and that no orthodoxy or gift can substitute for it.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "when that which is perfect is come" as the consummation, and "now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face" as the scriptural anchor for the direct vision of God given to the blessed. The contrast is between knowing in part now and knowing hereafter "even as also I am known," which is a mutual and immediate knowledge that no book, no doctrine, and no accumulation of study can supply. On this reading the retirement of prophecy, tongues, and knowledge belongs to the end of all things and not to the close of the apostolic age, so nothing in this passage announces that the charisms would be withdrawn from the Church in history. The verse also grounds a deep reserve about theological certainty in this life, since even revealed knowledge is described as partial and mirror-like until the vision itself is given.

counterpoint.summary: Most Protestant interpreters agree that "that which is perfect" is the eschaton, on the plain ground that "face to face" and knowing "even as also I am known" describe the presence of God rather than any development within church history. A cessationist minority reads the perfect as the completed canon or the church's maturity, arguing that once revelation was fully given in writing the revelatory gifts had served their purpose and would "fail" and "cease" of themselves. Continuationists reply that the childhood analogy describes a change of state rather than the arrival of a document, and that no reader in any century has experienced the sight this passage promises. Both sides accept the passage's main claim, that present knowledge is genuinely partial, and both use it to argue for humility about what we think we have understood.

verses.text: Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy.
For he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries.
But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort.
He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church.

I would that ye all spake with tongues, but rather that ye prophesied: for greater is he that prophesieth than he that speaketh with tongues, except he interpret, that the church may receive edifying.
Now, brethren, if I come unto you speaking with tongues, what shall I profit you, except I shall speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophesying, or by doctrine?
And even things without life giving sound, whether pipe or harp, except they give a distinction in the sounds, how shall it be known what is piped or harped?
For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
There are, it may be, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is without signification.
Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me.
Even so ye, forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual gifts, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church.
Wherefore let him that speaketh in an unknown tongue pray that he may interpret.
For if I pray in an unknown tongue, my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful.
What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.
Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?
For thou verily givest thanks well, but the other is not edified.
I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all:
Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men.
In the law it is written, With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord.
Wherefore tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not: but prophesying serveth not for them that believe not, but for them which believe.
If therefore the whole church be come together into one place, and all speak with tongues, and there come in those that are unlearned, or unbelievers, will they not say that ye are mad?
But if all prophesy, and there come in one that believeth not, or one unlearned, he is convinced of all, he is judged of all:
And thus are the secrets of his heart made manifest; and so falling down on his face he will worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth.
How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying.
If any man speak in an unknown tongue, let it be by two, or at the most by three, and that by course; and let one interpret.
But if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church; and let him speak to himself, and to God.
Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge.
If any thing be revealed to another that sitteth by, let the first hold his peace.
For ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted.
And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also saith the law.
And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home: for it is a shame for women to speak in the church.
What? came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only?
If any man think himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord.
But if any man be ignorant, let him be ignorant.
Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues.
Let all things be done decently and in order.

chapters.summary: The praise of charity turns immediately into instruction: "Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy." Both are commanded, but they are ranked, and the whole chapter explains the ranking by one criterion. An untranslated tongue is directed upward, since the speaker "speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth him; howbeit in the spirit he speaketh mysteries," while prophecy is directed outward, "unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort." The difference is stated as an audit: "He that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church." Paul is careful to concede rather than forbid — "I would that ye all spake with tongues, but rather that ye prophesied" — and he adds the qualifier that governs the rest, "except he interpret, that the church may receive edifying." Then come the sound analogies. A pipe or harp that gives no "distinction in the sounds" communicates nothing; "if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?"; unintelligible speech means "ye shall speak into the air." Every language in the world has meaning to someone, but "if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me." So the standard is fixed: "forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual gifts, seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church." Paul applies it even to prayer. The tongue-speaker should "pray that he may interpret," because "if I pray in an unknown tongue, my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful"; his resolution is to do both — "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also" — since otherwise the hearer "that occupieth the room of the unlearned" cannot "say Amen at thy giving of thanks." The thanksgiving may be excellent, "but the other is not edified." He then plays his strongest personal card and immediately spends it against himself: "I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all: Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue." A rebuke follows — "be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men" — supported by a citation, "With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak unto this people; and yet for all that will they not hear me, saith the Lord," from which Paul draws the conclusion that "tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not: but prophesying serveth not for them that believe not, but for them which believe." He then stages the scene twice. If outsiders arrive while "all speak with tongues," the verdict is "will they not say that ye are mad?" If instead "all prophesy," the unbeliever "is convinced of all, he is judged of all: And thus are the secrets of his heart made manifest; and so falling down on his face he will worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth." From there Paul legislates. The gathering he describes is fully participatory — "every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation" — under one rule, "Let all things be done unto edifying." Tongues are limited to "two, or at the most by three, and that by course; and let one interpret," and where there is no interpreter, "let him keep silence in the church; and let him speak to himself, and to God." Prophets likewise speak "two or three, and let the other judge," yielding to one another so that "if any thing be revealed to another that sitteth by, let the first hold his peace," because "ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted." The theological justification is compressed into two clauses: "the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" and "God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints." Then comes the disputed instruction, "Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak... And if they will learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home." Paul closes by puncturing Corinthian exceptionalism — "What? came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only?" — claiming apostolic authority for the whole set of rules, "let him acknowledge that the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord," dismissing further argument with "if any man be ignorant, let him be ignorant," and ending in balance: "covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues. Let all things be done decently and in order."
takeaways: One criterion runs through the entire chapter and settles every question in it: does the assembly understand, and is it built up. Paul states it as a command — "seek that ye may excel to the edifying of the church" — and repeats it as the rule over the whole gathering, "Let all things be done unto edifying." Intelligibility is not a concession to the slow or the unspiritual; it is the criterion by which a genuine gift is evaluated in public. The trumpet image makes the stakes plain, since "if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?" A signal nobody can read is not a superior signal but a failed one.

Paul never prohibits tongues; he ranks and regulates them, and he is scrupulous about saying so at both ends of the argument. He opens with "I would that ye all spake with tongues," claims "I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all," and closes with the direct command "forbid not to speak with tongues." What he denies is that a private benefit is automatically a public one, since "he that speaketh in an unknown tongue edifieth himself; but he that prophesieth edifieth the church." His own arithmetic is the sharpest statement of the ratio: "five words with my understanding" in the assembly are worth more than "ten thousand words in an unknown tongue."

Corporate worship is assessed by how it lands on the person who does not yet belong. Paul introduces two outsiders — the "unlearned" who cannot "say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest," and the unbeliever who walks in off the street — and the two outcomes he sketches could not be further apart. Untranslated ecstasy produces the verdict "ye are mad"; comprehensible prophecy produces conviction so exact that "the secrets of his heart made manifest," ending with a man "falling down on his face" to "worship God, and report that God is in you of a truth." A church's meeting is therefore a public act with evangelistic consequences, and self-absorbed worship forfeits them.

Inspiration, in Paul's account, does not suspend the speaker's responsibility. His rule that "the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" means the gift is under the control of the person who has it, which is why he can command a prophet mid-flow to "hold his peace" when "any thing be revealed to another that sitteth by," cap tongues at "two, or at the most by three," and impose silence where there is no interpreter. This removes the standard excuse for disorder. Nobody at Corinth could plead that the Spirit had overridden them, because the Spirit does not produce what "God is not the author of" — namely "confusion."

Prophecy is also placed under judgement rather than accepted uncritically: "Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge." A word claimed as revelation is to be weighed by the assembly, not received simply because it was delivered with confidence. Paired with the discerning of spirits named in the previous chapter, this establishes that the New Testament expects inspired speech to be tested in public, which is as much a protection of the congregation as it is a discipline on the speaker.

The order Paul imposes is theological rather than merely administrative, and it is deliberately not a demand for silence. He grounds it in God's own character, "God is not the author of confusion, but of peace," appeals beyond Corinth to the practice of "all churches of the saints," and punctures their sense of being a special case with "came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only?" Yet the same passage envisions a meeting where "every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation" and where "ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted." The final rule, "Let all things be done decently and in order," is stated positively for that reason: the regulation exists to make broad participation possible, not to shut it down.

crossRefs.label: Acts 2:4-11 — every man heard them speak in his own language... we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God
crossRefs.why: Pentecost is the founding instance of the gift Paul is regulating, and the contrast is the key to the chapter. There the tongues were immediately understood by foreigners and functioned as a sign to outsiders, exactly the role Paul assigns them when he says "tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not." At Corinth the same gift was producing the opposite effect, leaving hearers unable to say Amen, which is why Paul demands interpretation before it may be used in the assembly.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 28:11-12 — with stammering lips and another tongue will he speak to this people... yet they would not hear
crossRefs.why: This is the text Paul cites as "in the law it is written," and its original setting explains the sober conclusion he draws from it. Unintelligible speech there is a judgement on a people who refused plain instruction, not a reward for the spiritually advanced. Reading the source passage shows why Paul immediately warns "be not children in understanding" and why he treats a church full of uninterpreted tongues as a sign against itself rather than a mark of maturity.

crossRefs.label: Numbers 11:29 — would God that all the LORD’s people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit upon them
crossRefs.why: Moses refuses to restrict prophecy to an authorized circle when Joshua asks him to silence Eldad and Medad, and Paul's "ye may all prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be comforted" is the fulfilment of that wish under regulated conditions. The pairing shows that Paul's rules are not an attempt to narrow who may speak but a structure that lets many speak without the meeting dissolving.

crossRefs.label: Joel 2:28-29 — your sons and your daughters shall prophesy... upon the servants and upon the handmaids
crossRefs.why: The prophetic expectation Paul is operating inside explicitly includes daughters and handmaids among those who prophesy, which is why the silence instruction in this chapter has to be read against a wider background rather than in isolation. It also frames Paul's preference for prophecy as the characteristic gift of the age of the outpoured Spirit, available across the whole community rather than confined to a few.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 11:5 — every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered
crossRefs.why: Three chapters earlier Paul regulates how a woman prays and prophesies in the assembly rather than forbidding it, which creates the central interpretive problem of "Let your women keep silence in the churches." Any reading of chapter fourteen has to account for the fact that the same letter assumes women speaking prophetically in the same gathering, and the two passages are always argued together.

crossRefs.label: 1 Timothy 2:11-12 — I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man
crossRefs.why: The pastoral instruction supplies the closest parallel to the silence passage and is the text on which the debate over its scope usually turns, since it links silence to teaching and authority rather than to speech as such. Whether the two passages restrict the same activity, and how broadly, is the substance of the disagreement between complementarian and egalitarian readings.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading holds that the charisms described here have never been withdrawn from the Church. Paul's regulations presuppose gifts in active use and he ends by commanding "covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues," which is read as a standing instruction rather than a temporary arrangement for the apostolic generation. Extraordinary gifts are understood as genuinely possible in any age, given freely by the Spirit and not confined to the ordained, but they are always ordered to the building up of the whole body and always subject to discernment by those charged with the care of the Church, on the pattern Paul himself sets when he tells the assembly to "let the other judge." At the same time the tradition treats the ordinary means of grace — the sacraments, preaching, and the settled life of prayer — as the normal and primary way the Spirit sanctifies, so that the extraordinary charisms are welcomed as supplementary and tested rather than sought as the measure of spiritual attainment.

counterpoint.summary: Protestants are divided among themselves here more sharply than they are against Catholics. Cessationist readings hold that tongues and prophecy were revelatory sign-gifts attesting the apostolic message, pointing to Paul's own statement that "tongues are for a sign, not to them that believe, but to them that believe not," and argue that once the apostolic revelation was complete the gifts served no further purpose and ceased, as the previous chapter said they would; on this view continuing prophecy would compete with the finality and sufficiency of Scripture. Pentecostal and charismatic readings answer that the text sets no expiry date, that "forbid not to speak with tongues" is a plain command, and that Paul assumes tongues in private prayer where "my spirit prayeth, but my understanding is unfruitful"; many hold tongues to be associated with a baptism in the Holy Spirit, and treat contemporary prophecy as non-canonical edification that must itself be judged by Scripture. Reformed and evangelical interpreters occupy a spectrum in between, often described as open but cautious. Every side agrees on what Paul actually legislates: whatever operates must be intelligible, limited in number, interpreted, judged, and directed at the edification of the church rather than the display of the speaker.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic reading, "Let all things be done decently and in order" establishes that public worship belongs to the Church as a body and is not the property of whoever feels moved. Paul does not merely advise; he legislates numbers, sequence, interpretation, and silence, and he closes the case with a claim of binding authority — "the things that I write unto you are the commandments of the Lord" — while measuring Corinth against the common practice of "all churches of the saints." That combination of apostolic command and inter-church uniformity is read as the seed of liturgical order: worship is a received and regulated act, entrusted to the Church's pastors to arrange, in which the community's prayer has a shape that does not depend on the temperament of individuals. The "Amen" of the one "that occupieth the room of the unlearned" is heard as the congregation's own assent to a public thanksgiving, which is why the thanksgiving must be offered in words the people can follow.

counterpoint.summary: Protestants agree that order is commanded and that Paul writes with binding authority, but they divide over how far the chapter licenses developed ceremonial. On the regulative principle, only what Scripture positively warrants belongs in worship, so this chapter functions as a prescriptive list — reading, teaching, prayer, singing, thanksgiving with an intelligible Amen — and the burden falls on anyone adding to it. On the normative principle, whatever Scripture does not forbid may be ordered by the church in Christian liberty, which allows for liturgical development while keeping edification as the test. Many Protestant readers also press the picture in the middle of the chapter, where "every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation," and argue that a service in which the congregation only listens is as distant from Paul's meeting as chaos is. Both traditions hold that worship is God-ordered rather than improvised, that it must be conducted in words the people can understand well enough to say Amen, and that its purpose is the building up of the assembly.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "Let your women keep silence in the churches" as a restricted rather than absolute prohibition, because the same letter has already regulated the manner in which "every woman that prayeth or prophesieth" does so, and Paul cannot be forbidding in chapter fourteen what he assumed in chapter eleven. The silence is therefore understood of a particular function in the assembly: most naturally the authoritative public judging of prophecy that Paul has just described in "let the other judge," together with the official liturgical proclamation and teaching that belongs to the ordained ministry. The tradition reads the passage as reflecting a real ordering within the assembly rather than a judgement on women's capacity, holding at the same time that women have genuinely received the charisms, have prophesied, have taught in many settings, and stand among the Church's greatest saints and doctors, while the sacramental office of presbyter and bishop remains reserved.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings split on this text as sharply as on any in the letter. Complementarian interpreters take the instruction as permanently binding in substance, restricting the authoritative teaching and the official evaluation of prophecy in the gathered church, and read it alongside "I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man," while agreeing with the Catholic point that chapter eleven prevents it from meaning total silence. Egalitarian interpreters press the same tension in the opposite direction and offer several accounts: that what is forbidden is disruptive interrogation during the meeting, which fits the remedy "let them ask their husbands at home"; that the instruction addresses a specific local situation of untrained hearers rather than a universal rule; or that the appeal to what the law "saith" is Paul quoting a Corinthian position which he then demolishes with "What? came the word of God out from you? or came it unto you only?" A minority argue on manuscript grounds that the verses are a later insertion. All parties concede that the passage cannot be read flatly without contradicting 1 Corinthians 11, and all must give some account of how women prophesying and women keeping silence belong in the same letter.

verses.text: Moreover, brethren, I declare unto you the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand;
By which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.
For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures;
And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:
And that he was seen of Cephas, then of the twelve:
After that, he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present, but some are fallen asleep.
After that, he was seen of James; then of all the apostles.
And last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time.
For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.
But by the grace of God I am what I am: and his grace which was bestowed upon me was not in vain; but I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
Therefore whether it were I or they, so we preach, and so ye believed.
Now if Christ be preached that he rose from the dead, how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?
But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen:
And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain.
Yea, and we are found false witnesses of God; because we have testified of God that he raised up Christ: whom he raised not up, if so be that the dead rise not.
For if the dead rise not, then is not Christ raised:
And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins.
Then they also which are fallen asleep in Christ are perished.
If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.
But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.
For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead.
For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
But every man in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming.
Then cometh the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father; when he shall have put down all rule and all authority and power.
For he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet.
The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.
For he hath put all things under his feet. But when he saith all things are put under him, it is manifest that he is excepted, which did put all things under him.
And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all.
Else what shall they do which are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all? why are they then baptized for the dead?
And why stand we in jeopardy every hour?
I protest by your rejoicing which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily.
If after the manner of men I have fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantageth it me, if the dead rise not? let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die.
Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.
Awake to righteousness, and sin not; for some have not the knowledge of God: I speak this to your shame.
But some man will say, How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?
Thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die:
And that which thou sowest, thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain, it may chance of wheat, or of some other grain:
But God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body.
All flesh is not the same flesh: but there is one kind of flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds.
There are also celestial bodies, and bodies terrestrial: but the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another.
There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory.
So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption:
It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power:
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.
And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.
Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual.
The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven.
As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.
And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.
Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption.
Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.
For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.
So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.
O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law.
But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

chapters.summary: Paul turns from disorder in the assembly to the foundation underneath everything he has argued, reminding the Corinthians of “the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand,” by which they are saved “if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.” What he hands on he first received: “how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.” Then the witnesses are counted out one after another — “seen of Cephas, then of the twelve,” “of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present,” “of James; then of all the apostles,” and “last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time,” by a man who calls himself “the least of the apostles” because “I persecuted the church of God,” yet who can say “by the grace of God I am what I am.” Only then does the problem surface: “how say some among you that there is no resurrection of the dead?” Paul runs that denial to its end without softening it. “If there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen”; preaching is vain and faith is vain; the apostles are “found false witnesses of God”; “ye are yet in your sins”; those “fallen asleep in Christ are perished”; and “if in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.” Against that ruin he sets one sentence: “But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.” Two men are set head to head — “for as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” — and an order is laid out: “Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming,” then “the end,” when the kingdom is delivered up and “all rule and all authority and power” put down, for “he must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet,” and “the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death,” until at last “God may be all in all.” Practical arguments follow in quick succession: the much-disputed “what shall they do which are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all?”; Paul’s own exposure, “why stand we in jeopardy every hour?” and “I die daily”; his fight “with beasts at Ephesus”; and the only honest alternative if the grave is final, “let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die.” He breaks off into warning — “evil communications corrupt good manners” — and summons: “Awake to righteousness, and sin not; for some have not the knowledge of God: I speak this to your shame.” To the sceptic’s question, “How are the dead raised up? and with what body do they come?”, he answers with seed and starlight. What is sown “is not quickened, except it die,” and “thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain,” while “God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body.” As “one star differeth from another star in glory,” so the risen body differs from the buried one: “it is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.” The two Adams frame the whole — “the first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit,” “the first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven” — and the promise is that “as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.” The chapter ends in mystery and trumpet. “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption,” yet “we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump,” when “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality,” and the old word comes true: “Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” Because “the sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law,” the thanks belong wholly to God “which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” — and the argument lands, characteristically, as a command to keep working: “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.”
takeaways: Paul introduces the resurrection not as his insight but as a delivery: “I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received.” He presents himself as a link in a chain rather than an origin, and the content he passes on is already fixed and confessional in shape — died for our sins, was buried, rose the third day, was seen. That handing-on is what makes the gospel checkable: he can name Cephas, the twelve, James, “above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present,” effectively inviting anyone who doubts to go and ask them. And it is not merely informational, since salvation is bound to holding it fast: they are saved “if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.”

The chain of consequences in verses 13-19 refuses to let the resurrection be an optional appendix to Christian faith. If the dead are not raised, then Christ is not raised; if Christ is not raised, “then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain”; worse, the apostles are “found false witnesses of God,” not merely mistaken but slanderers of him. Most striking is what Paul says collapses next: “ye are yet in your sins.” Forgiveness is not something the cross secures independently of Easter and to which the resurrection merely adds confirmation. And the honest conclusion, if it were all untrue, is not a diminished but still admirable religion — it is that “we are of all men most miserable.”

“Firstfruits” is a harvest word, and Paul leans on everything it implies: “now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.” The first sheaf is not a different crop from the rest but the same crop arriving early, so Christ’s risen body is a specimen of what is promised rather than a unique exception to the rule of death. From this comes both a sequence — “Christ the firstfruits; afterward they that are Christ’s at his coming” — and a destination, since “the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death” and the reign of the Son ends not in his own aggrandizement but “that God may be all in all.” Christian hope here is not escape from embodiment but the abolition of the thing that ends embodied life.

Asked “with what body do they come?” Paul neither retreats into a bodiless afterlife nor promises a mere resuscitation of the corpse. The seed answers both errors at once: “that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die,” and “thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain.” There is real continuity — the same seed, “to every seed his own body” — and real transformation, hammered out in four matched pairs: “sown in corruption... raised in incorruption... sown in dishonour... raised in glory... sown in weakness... raised in power... sown a natural body... raised a spiritual body.” The “spiritual body” is not a body made of spirit but a body wholly answerable to the Spirit, which is why “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” denies the survival of mortality, not of matter.

The chapter’s anthropology is corporate before it is individual. Every human being is described as wearing a likeness received from another: “the first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit,” and “as is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.” Death is therefore not a private biological fact but an inheritance — “since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead” — and glory is likewise received rather than achieved: “as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.” Solidarity with Adam is unchosen; solidarity with Christ is offered.

The most abstract chapter Paul ever wrote ends with a work order. “Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.” The word “vain” has been the chapter’s refrain — preaching vain, faith vain, believing in vain — and it is now decisively negated on the other side. If the body has a future, then what is done in the body is not wasted motion, and the contrary slogan Paul quoted, “let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die,” is exposed as the only rational ethic for people with no resurrection. Doctrine here is not the opposite of practicality; it is what makes endurance reasonable.

crossRefs.label: Romans 5:12-21 — as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin
crossRefs.why: Paul works out at length there the head-to-head comparison he states in compressed form here, “for as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.” Reading the two together shows that the resurrection argument rests on a doctrine of representation: death spread through one man’s act, and life is conveyed the same way, which is why Christ’s rising is not an isolated marvel but the beginning of a race’s reversal.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 25:8 — He will swallow up death in victory
crossRefs.why: Paul’s climactic “then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory” quotes this promise directly. In its own setting it belongs to a feast on the mountain for all peoples, where God wipes away tears from every face, so Paul is claiming that the general resurrection is the fulfilment of a hope Israel already held rather than a new idea imported into the faith.

crossRefs.label: Hosea 13:14 — O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction
crossRefs.why: The taunt Paul raises over the emptied grave, “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”, is drawn from this oracle of ransom from the power of the grave. Set beside the prophet’s words, Paul’s question is not a rhetorical flourish but the mockery of a defeated enemy whose destruction God had already announced.

crossRefs.label: Daniel 12:2-3 — many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake... shall shine as the brightness of the firmament
crossRefs.why: Two of this chapter’s central images are already joined here: sleep as the figure for death, which Paul uses of those “fallen asleep in Christ,” and astral glory for the risen righteous, which stands behind “one star differeth from another star in glory.” The prophecy also holds together resurrection and judgment, which is the framework within which Paul places the delivering up of the kingdom.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 3:21 — Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body
crossRefs.why: This states in one line what the seed analogy argues at length, that the same body is changed rather than discarded, and it identifies the pattern of the change as Christ’s own risen body. It confirms that “we shall also bear the image of the heavenly” means conformity to a particular person and not absorption into a general spiritual condition.

crossRefs.label: 2 Maccabees 12:43-45 — in that he was mindful of the resurrection... it had been superfluous and vain to pray for the dead
crossRefs.why: This passage joins the same two convictions Paul joins in the puzzling verse about those “baptized for the dead”: that the dead will rise, and that the living may act religiously on their behalf. Whatever the Corinthian practice was, the pairing was not unheard of in the Jewish world Paul came from, and this text is where the Catholic tradition finds the clearest scriptural precedent for it.

interpretationNotes.claim: On “Else what shall they do which are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all? why are they then baptized for the dead?”, the Catholic reading grants that Paul neither describes the practice nor commends it, and the tradition has never taught a vicarious sacrament administered to the living on behalf of the departed. What it does take from the verse is the underlying assumption Paul finds unremarkable enough to argue from: that there is a real bond between the living Church and the dead, and that what the living do can bear on the state of those who have died. That conviction is what the communion of saints names, and it is why prayer, almsgiving, and above all the offering of the Eucharist for the departed are regarded as ancient and coherent rather than as later accretions. The argument only works, Paul says, because the dead rise; the same logic supports intercession for them, since one does not pray for those with no future.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters emphasize Paul’s grammar: he says “they” and not “we,” shifting to the first person only in the next breath with “why stand we in jeopardy every hour?” On the common reading this is an argument from an opponent’s inconsistency — some in Corinth were doing something that presupposed a future for the dead while others denied that future — and Paul exploits the contradiction without approving the rite. More broadly, Protestant theology holds that each person is judged on the basis of Christ’s finished work received by faith in this life, so no sacrament and no prayer can transfer benefit across death, and a verse this obscure cannot establish a practice the rest of Scripture never commands. Both traditions agree on what the verse assumes and what it is used to prove: that the resurrection of the dead is real, and that any practice premised on the dead having no future is incoherent for a Christian.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads the chapter’s account of glory as graded and as requiring a real fitness in the one glorified. “There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory” is taken to describe not only the difference between earthly and heavenly bodies but genuine degrees of beatitude among the saved, corresponding to the charity in which each died — which is why the chapter can close by insisting that “your labour is not in vain in the Lord.” Alongside this, “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption” is read as stating an absolute condition: nothing corruptible passes into glory. Since many die genuinely in grace yet still attached to sin and unfree of its residue, the tradition concludes that a final purification completes what grace began, so that the incorruption Paul describes is not a legal exemption from holiness but its actual attainment.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings answer that Paul locates the whole change in a single divine act at the end: “we shall all be changed, In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump.” An instantaneous transformation wrought by God at the trumpet leaves no room and no need for an intervening process undergone by the soul, and the chapter never hints at one. The heavenly bodies in verses 40-41 are ordinarily read as an argument about God’s freedom in fitting bodies to their spheres — he “giveth it a body as it hath pleased him” — rather than as a taxonomy of rewards, and “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” is read as a statement about mortality, not about unpurged guilt. The believer’s title to glory is Christ’s righteousness received by faith, and glorification is God’s immediate completion of that gift. Both traditions affirm that nothing unfit enters the kingdom, that the fitting is God’s work and not the creature’s achievement, and that what is raised is transformed rather than merely revived.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes seriously the conditional Paul attaches to salvation in the opening lines: they are saved by the gospel “if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.” Faith is presented as something that can be held and also let go, and believing itself can turn out to have been in vain, which supports the tradition’s teaching that justification once received can be lost through grave sin or apostasy and that perseverance is a gift to be prayed for rather than a possession already secured. The chapter’s last verse is read in the same key: the exhortation to be “stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” is given a motive — “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” — so that works done in grace genuinely count toward the glory that follows rather than merely evidencing a verdict already fixed.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters divide here, though less sharply than the caricature suggests. Those holding that the elect necessarily persevere read “unless ye have believed in vain” as describing faith that was never genuine, an empty profession exposed by its failure to hold, and they point out that Paul’s very next move is to attribute everything he is and does to grace — “by the grace of God I am what I am” — which is also how perseverance itself is supplied. Those holding that a real believer may fall away read the conditional much as the Catholic tradition does, while still denying that continuance is a work the believer contributes. On the closing verse, Protestant readings generally take “your labour is not in vain in the Lord” as a promise of God’s gracious reward for work he himself enables, not as merit strictly owed. Both traditions agree that the warning is meant to be heard as a warning, that a faith which does not endure does not save, and that whatever endurance the Christian has is grace at work.

verses.text: Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I have given order to the churches of Galatia, even so do ye.
Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come.
And when I come, whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters, them will I send to bring your liberality unto Jerusalem.
And if it be meet that I go also, they shall go with me.
Now I will come unto you, when I shall pass through Macedonia: for I do pass through Macedonia.
And it may be that I will abide, yea, and winter with you, that ye may bring me on my journey whithersoever I go.
For I will not see you now by the way; but I trust to tarry a while with you, if the Lord permit.
But I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost.
For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.
Now if Timotheus come, see that he may be with you without fear: for he worketh the work of the Lord, as I also do.
Let no man therefore despise him: but conduct him forth in peace, that he may come unto me: for I look for him with the brethren.
As touching our brother Apollos, I greatly desired him to come unto you with the brethren: but his will was not at all to come at this time; but he will come when he shall have convenient time.
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Let all your things be done with charity.
I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,)
That ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth.
I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied.
For they have refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such.
The churches of Asia salute you. Aquila and Priscilla salute you much in the Lord, with the church that is in their house.
All the brethren greet you. Greet ye one another with an holy kiss.
The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand.
If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha.
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.

chapters.summary: One verse after the last trumpet, Paul is talking about money. “Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I have given order to the churches of Galatia, even so do ye” — and the order is unglamorously concrete: “Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come.” Everyone gives, the amount is proportioned to what each has received, the habit is weekly rather than impulsive, and the point of the discipline is that nothing be scrambled together at the last moment under the pressure of an apostle’s presence. Nor will Paul touch it alone: the Corinthians themselves will choose the couriers, “whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters,” to carry “your liberality unto Jerusalem,” and he will accompany them only “if it be meet that I go also.” Travel plans follow, held with open hands. He will come “when I shall pass through Macedonia”; he may “abide, yea, and winter with you”; he hopes “to tarry a while with you, if the Lord permit”; but for now “I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost,” and the reason he gives is both invitation and hazard in one breath: “For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.” Then people. Timothy is commended to a congregation Paul evidently fears may bruise him — “see that he may be with you without fear: for he worketh the work of the Lord, as I also do. Let no man therefore despise him: but conduct him forth in peace” — and Apollos, whose name had been made a party banner at Corinth, is reported as freely declining: “I greatly desired him to come unto you with the brethren: but his will was not at all to come at this time.” Sixteen chapters of correction then compress into five short imperatives and one governing qualifier: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. Let all your things be done with charity.” The household of Stephanas is held up as the pattern of the leadership the church actually needs, “the firstfruits of Achaia” who “have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,” and the congregation is told, “That ye submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth.” Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus have arrived and “refreshed my spirit and yours: therefore acknowledge ye them that are such.” Greetings come from “the churches of Asia” and from “Aquila and Priscilla... with the church that is in their house,” with the charge to “greet ye one another with an holy kiss.” Paul then takes the pen from the scribe — “the salutation of me Paul with mine own hand” — and in his own writing sets down a line of startling severity beside a word of longing: “If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha.” The letter that opened by rebuking a church split into factions closes without a single condition attached: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.”
takeaways: The collection is administered with a care that borders on the bureaucratic, and that is deliberate. “Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him” makes giving universal, regular, and proportional rather than exceptional and emotional, while “that there be no gatherings when I come” removes the apostle’s personal pressure from the moment of giving. Most telling is the handling of the funds: the Corinthians choose the carriers, “whomsoever ye shall approve by your letters,” and Paul travels with them only if it seems fitting. A man who could have claimed unquestioned authority over the money instead builds a structure in which he is never alone with it.

The day named is not incidental. Immediately after a chapter arguing that everything rests on Christ having “rose again the third day,” Paul assumes without explanation that “the first day of the week” is the natural rhythm of the Corinthians’ common life. The resurrection is not merely something they believe; it has already reshaped their calendar, so that the day the tomb was found empty is the day on which their charity is organized. Doctrine and habit are the same fabric here, which is why the transition from the last trumpet to a weekly envelope is not a change of subject.

Paul’s plans are stated firmly and held loosely at once. He intends to winter at Corinth and to stay until Pentecost at Ephesus, yet everything is subordinated to “if the Lord permit.” And his reason for staying is a sentence that refuses the usual logic of guidance: “for a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.” The opposition is not evidence that the door is shut; the two arrive together, and the second clause is offered as part of the case for remaining rather than as a reason to leave.

Two co-workers are handled in ways that quietly undo the party spirit the letter opened by attacking. Timothy, younger and evidently vulnerable at Corinth, is given apostolic cover — “see that he may be with you without fear... Let no man therefore despise him” — with the ground being simply that “he worketh the work of the Lord, as I also do.” Apollos, whose name some Corinthians had adopted as a faction label, is shown declining Paul’s own urging: “his will was not at all to come at this time.” Paul neither commands him nor resents him. The men the Corinthians were setting against each other are visibly not competing.

The whole letter is compressed into five imperatives and then immediately qualified: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. Let all your things be done with charity.” The four commands before it are vigilant, immovable, courageous, and strong — the vocabulary of a garrison — and the Corinthians were a church quite capable of being all four in the service of their own quarrels. The last sentence governs the rest. Not some of your things and not chiefly your religious things, but “all your things,” done in the manner set out earlier in the letter, where charity is what makes every gift worth having.

Authority in the closing paragraph is grounded entirely in labour freely undertaken. The household of Stephanas “have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,” and precisely because of that the congregation is told to “submit yourselves unto such, and to every one that helpeth with us, and laboureth.” No title is mentioned, no appointment recounted; the claim rests on having given themselves away and having “refreshed my spirit and yours.” The instruction “acknowledge ye them that are such” makes recognition a duty owed by the church, not a favour granted — the exact inverse of a community that had been choosing its leaders by eloquence and preference.

crossRefs.label: Romans 15:26-27 — a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem
crossRefs.why: This is the same relief fund seen from a later stage of the project, and it supplies the theology Paul leaves unstated here: the Gentile churches are “debtors” because “if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, their duty is also to minister unto them in carnal things.” The weekly envelope at Corinth turns out to be an argument about the unity of Jew and Gentile in one body, carried in coin.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 8:20-21 — Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men
crossRefs.why: Paul later spells out the motive behind the procedure sketched here, that approved delegates carry the money so that “no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us.” Read together, the two passages show that the choosing of couriers “by your letters” is a deliberate safeguard of transparency rather than a mere convenience of travel.

crossRefs.label: Acts 20:7 — upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread
crossRefs.why: Luke records as ordinary practice the assembly that Paul here assumes when he tells the Corinthians to set money aside “upon the first day of the week.” Taken together, the two texts are the earliest plain evidence that the churches gathered on the day of the resurrection, and that the gathering had both a table and a common purse attached to it.

crossRefs.label: Acts 19 — all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus... and the same time there arose no small stir about that way
crossRefs.why: Luke’s account of Ephesus gives both halves of Paul’s remark that “a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries”: two years of daily teaching that reached a whole province, and a riot that nearly cost him his life. It also explains why he writes from Ephesus and delays his visit rather than abandoning the city.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 1:12,16 — I am of Paul; and I of Apollos... And I baptized also the household of Stephanas
crossRefs.why: The letter’s opening complaint and its closing commendations answer each other. The names used as faction banners at the start reappear at the end as men who cooperate and defer, and Stephanas, mentioned in chapter one only as someone Paul happened to baptize, is now the model of the service the whole church is told to honour.

crossRefs.label: Revelation 22:20 — Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus
crossRefs.why: The cry embedded in Paul’s “Anathema Maranatha” is the same longing with which the New Testament itself closes, and both stand immediately before a final benediction of grace. The parallel shows that the appeal to the Lord’s coming functions as prayer and as warning at once, depending entirely on whether the one who hears it loves him.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading treats “upon the first day of the week” as more than a convenient scheduling detail. Paul gives the same order to Galatia and to Corinth, assumes without argument that the churches are already assembling on that day, and attaches an act of corporate charity to it, which the tradition takes as evidence that the Lord’s Day was from the beginning a fixed assembly centred on the resurrection and on the breaking of bread rather than a private convention. From this the Catholic tradition draws a further conclusion: the observance of Sunday rests on the apostolic practice of the Church, handed on and made binding by her authority, rather than on any written command transferring the Sabbath. That the day of obligation is Sunday and not the seventh day is therefore itself an instance of the Church ordering the life of the faithful under apostolic warrant, and the duty to keep it is a genuine obligation of worship rather than a mere custom.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters largely agree that the first day was already distinctive because of the resurrection, but they ground its observance in Scripture rather than in ecclesial authority, treating the apostolic pattern recorded in the New Testament as itself the warrant. Within that, they divide. Some hold a transfer of the Sabbath commandment to the first day, so that Sunday carries the moral weight of the fourth commandment. Others hold that no day binds the Christian conscience, appealing to Paul’s own insistence elsewhere that days are not to be made a test of standing, and reading Sunday gathering as an excellent and apostolic custom rather than a precept. A number also note that the instruction here is that each one “lay by him in store,” which reads most naturally as setting something aside at home, so that the verse establishes the rhythm of the week more clearly than it establishes the liturgy of the assembly. Both traditions agree that the first day is the resurrection day, that the earliest churches met on it, and that Christian giving belongs to the ordinary rhythm of worship rather than to emergencies.

interpretationNotes.claim: On “If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha,” Catholic reading hears the language of formal exclusion. Anathema in the Church’s later usage became the technical word for a solemn sentence separating someone from the communion of the faithful, and the tradition sees its root here and in Paul’s comparable language elsewhere: the Church, exercising a real authority given to her, may declare that a person has placed himself outside the body. The pairing with maranatha is read as placing that judgment under the Lord’s own coming, which keeps the sentence from being merely punitive — exclusion is medicinal, aimed at repentance before the day when the Lord himself judges, and it can always be lifted when the one excluded returns. Read this way, the verse belongs with the earlier chapters of the letter where Paul instructs the assembled church to act judicially in a case of grave sin.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the line as a solemn declaration rather than the institution of a juridical censure. Paul is not pronouncing sentence on a named person but stating the condition of anyone whose heart is not set on Christ: such a one is already accursed, and the coming of the Lord will disclose it. On this reading the verse defines the boundary of the church by love for Christ rather than by an official act, and it functions as a final searching appeal to the reader. Where discipline is concerned, Protestant traditions locate the authority in the congregation or its elders acting under the Word, exercised through admonition and exclusion from the table, and always reversible upon repentance; they resist making anathema a formal power resident in an office. Both traditions agree that the words are severe and meant to be, that real exclusion from the fellowship is sometimes necessary, and that the final verdict is the Lord’s and not the Church’s.
